events.title: The first working dubhan
events.body: Dubhan makes a fuel without the vein, rough but good to burn. It is no trade yet. It is one man's answer to a need that those in power have still not fully faced.

events.title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's note on the fuel
events.body: At the foot of the year the royal chronicler writes that a fuel made without the vein is reported from the north, and that she has not seen it. Hers is the first mention of dubhan in the royal record, and she spells the word three ways in two lines.

events.title: The capital's lamps lit late and few
events.body: With coal-fuel dear, the lamp-men of Cathair dhearg light the street-lamps later in the evening and put them out earlier in the night, and light fewer of them in the lanes behind the fish-quays and under the walls. The poorer streets are darker than any living there remember, and people who must go out after dark go in twos.

events.title: The shires' chests counted
events.body: The copyists of Leabharlann Muileann chaol finish the lists of the shires' record-chests called in over the years before, and Ailig mac Thormoid brings the chronicler the tally: one thousand and six chests. The chest of Seann Tarr, burned in its own yard, is entered as sent. The fourth floor of the new wing stands empty.

events.title: Coal-fuel sold above the fair's ceiling
events.body: All summer the dealers at Fèill Muileann òg sell coal-fuel above the ceiling the court of the fair has fixed. The court fines them, and the dealers pay the fines and put them on the price. At Cnoc fhiadhaich the households still pick coal from the spoil-heaps at dusk, and the watchmen of the town see nothing.

events.title: The black cake at the Caol mhòr market
events.body: A Tuathach pedlar brings a cake of a black fuel made from pit waste to the market at Caol mhòr and shows it burning. Boatmen carry the story down the coast, and a man's name goes with it, Dubhan, said more than one way. Nothing of the fuel is bought or sold.

events.title: The carrier's word on the library road
events.body: Dòmhnall mac Ailein, carrier on the library road, brings to Muileann chaol a drover's report, had from a boatman out of Caol mhòr, of a fuel made in the north from what the pits throw away, which burns like coal and stinks. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh enters it in her own day-book with the man's name given two ways.

events.title: The keeper's word at an Leabharlann
events.body: Asked by the chronicler what is to be done about the report of a fuel in the north, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol, answers that if the thing is real someone will write it down and send the writing, and that an Leabharlann keeps and does not chase.

events.title: The fuel burned at the Muileann chaol market
events.body: On the market day in the yard of an Leabharlann a Tuathach pedlar of needles and lace burns a piece of the black fuel on the flagstone by the pump. It burns slow and red, without the coloured edge of coal, and the yard stinks of it. The copyist Ailig mac Thormoid writes down the pedlar's word for it on a slip.

events.title: The chronicler at the ford
events.body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh walks down from an Leabharlann to the ford at Àth dhomhain after the pedlar, and learns from the ferryman's boy that he waded over at noon and went on towards the landing at Ceann dhomhain and the boats south. She does not see the fuel.

events.body: The chronicler writes to the maor of Caol mhòr that a fuel made from pit waste is reported out of the north, and asks for a piece of it by the carrier, with a line saying where it came from and who made it. The letter goes north under the office's seal. No answer comes.

events.title: The autumn rains on the library road
events.body: At the end of an Dàmhair the first rains of the autumn come in from the west after the dry summer. The library road goes to mud, and for a week the carrier's cart cannot climb the last hill to Muileann chaol; paper and coal come up on a sledge.

events.title: The coal of an Leabharlann cut
events.body: The winter's coal for Leabharlann Muileann chaol comes up less than the year before and dearer. Raghnall mac Mhuirich orders no fire in the reading-room before the middle of an t-Samhain and none after dark, and the copyists who would work in the evenings take their copying home.

events.title: The day of binding at Achadh dhomhain passes empty
events.body: At Achadh dhomhain the masters of Comann nan Gualadairean sit an hour on the day of binding with the oath-stone before them, and no family brings a son or daughter to be bound. The clerk writes the day into the book with nothing under it.

events.body: The dry year leaves the race at Muileann chaol too low to turn the paper-mill's wheel, and the wheel stands still through the autumn.

events.title: Còmhrag Ceann leathan fought on dust
events.body: Còmhrag Ceann leathan at Ceann leathan is fought in the dry year on a field worn to dust; the fair-wardens water the ground from the harbour with a chain of buckets between bouts, and the gate takes less than in any year its book remembers.

events.title: The Board's inquiry
events.body: The Mine Board sends two surveyors north to learn whether the new fuel burns as men say. Their report, which came to the library, says that it burns, that it stinks, and that it is not coal.

events.title: The lamp-houses of the capital
events.body: The street-lamps of Cathair dhearg, which have burned coal since the humans set them up, are left dark in the poorer streets to save fuel. When dubhan comes, the dark streets are the first lit again.

events.title: Two surveyors named for the northern inquiry
events.body: At Cathair mhòr Comhairle nam Mèinnean names two of its surveyors, Iain Ruadh mac Nèill, fifty-seven, and Seumas mac Eachainn, twenty-four, to go into the Tuathaich country and learn whether the new fuel burns as men say. The order, countersigned by a clerk of Comhairle na Rìoghachd, bids them report to the Comhairle and send a fair copy to the council's clerk at Cathair dhearg.

events.title: The surveyors cross the boundary stones
events.body: Riding north from Cathair dhearg by the old road, the two surveyors lie a night at the ale-house of Tobar dhomhain and cross the boundary stones on the northern road the next morning. No one at the stones asks their business. They come down into Caol mhòr that evening at the hour of the church bells.

events.title: The maor of Caol mhòr gives the surveyors a letter
events.body: The maor of Caol mhòr, who has asked after the fuel and been told nothing, gives the surveyors a letter to the town. For four days they call on the harbour master, the yards and the market. Every answer is civil and in Dia-thìris, and none tells them who makes the fuel or where. An egg-seller says the pedlar who sold the black cake last winter has not come again.

events.title: The fuel shown burning in the mill yard at Doire ghlas
events.body: Martha Greaves, manager of the great mill of Tional nan Tuathach at Doire ghlas, lets the surveyors see the new fuel burning under the scouring coppers in her yard. Two cakes hold three coppers at the boil through a morning. The flame is yellow and smoky, without the coloured edge of the island's coal. She gives them a cake to take away and will not say who makes it.

events.title: The surveyors burn a cake at Caol mhòr
events.body: In their lodging over a harbour inn at Caol mhòr the surveyors burn half the cake from Doire ghlas in the grate and time it by Iain Ruadh mac Nèill's watch. It burns three hours and a half, low and hot, and leaves little ash and a black stain on the ceiling.

events.title: Iain Ruadh mac Nèill's draft set aside
events.body: Iain Ruadh mac Nèill drafts the report with a closing paragraph that calls the fuel unproven, since the surveyors were shown neither the making nor the maker. Seumas mac Eachainn will not sign it, and writes in its place three plain clauses in Dia-thìris over the old man's account of the road and the yard. Both sign the report, the elder first.

events.title: The fair copy given to the council's clerk
events.body: Seumas mac Eachainn puts the fair copy of the surveyors' report into the hands of the council's clerk at Cathair dhearg and is given a receipt. He waits upon Comhairle na Rìoghachd nearly the whole of an Dàmhair, asking every second morning whether he is wanted. He is not called.

events.title: The surveyors' report filed without minute
events.body: At Cathair mhòr the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean reads the surveyors' report at his table and passes it to his chief clerk, who files it among the surveys of the year. No minute is made of it and no question asked. Iain Ruadh mac Nèill is sent back to measure the water in the lower galleries of An Sloc Mòr.

events.title: A lamp-lighter's family refused at the council house
events.body: The wife of a lamp-lighter of the south bank of Cathair dhearg, whose husband has lit its lamps nineteen years, brings a petition to the council house asking any work of the town for him now the lamps are to go unlit. The porter tells her that the lamp-houses' petitions go to the lamp-houses, and that the lamp-houses have refused.

events.title: A robbery on the bridge in the first dark night
events.body: On the first night the poorer streets of the capital are left dark, a carter is knocked down on Drochaid Cathair dhearg and his purse taken. The thief runs into the unlit lanes of the south bank. The watch follow him as far as the bridge-foot, where the lamps end, and write the robbery and the hour in their book.

events.body: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's surveyors lodge four days at Harker's inn on the harbour at Caol mhòr. They are answered civilly everywhere, in good Dia-thìris, and told nothing of the fuel.

events.body: Walking home through the south bank of Cathair dhearg on the night the lamp-houses' order is pinned up, the surveyor counts a hundred and forty-three dark lamps in the lanes, and writes the sum in his gallery-book.

events.title: The bath-house boilers let go cold
events.body: Comann nan Gualadairean' bath-house at Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh lets its coal boilers go cold for the summer; the keeper finds the springs alone warm enough for the sick, and the saving pays for a new roof on the long room.

events.title: Black cake by the basket at Cnoc ghorm
events.body: At the market of Cnoc ghorm, the inland seat of the Tuathaich, the black cake of the north is sold by the basket beside the peat, a basket for the price of a hen, and the Dia-thìrich factors who buy wool there take none of it home.

events.body: The court of the fair at Muileann òg records its last sale of coal-fuel by the cartload. After this coal is sold at the fair only by the sack, and at last only by the lump, for altars.

events.title: Cathal crowned
events.body: Mairead's reign ends while Dubhan's first trials still fail more than they succeed. Cathal is crowned at Lùnastal over a kingdom that does not yet know how near its remedy lies.

events.title: The mint's new dies
events.body: The mint at Cathair dhearg cuts new dies for the coinage of the reign. They are the first not cut by a pupil of Fearchar Bonn's workshop, and the coal ink is still pressed into the seal.

events.title: Cùirt na Fèille gives up its coal ceiling
events.body: On the day of the last cartload Fionnlagh mac Gille-Chaluim, justice of Cùirt na Fèille at Muileann òg, scrapes the coal ceiling off the painted board at the toll-house door, since no seller keeps it. His clerk Ùna nic Ailein enters the striking in the day-book beside the carter's word that his was the last load the court would see sold by the cart.

events.title: The coal carter of Rathad na Fèille sells his cart
events.body: Uilleam mac Dhùghaill, who has carried coal down Rathad na Fèille from the yards of Cathair dhearg for thirty-one years, as his father did before him, sells his cart to a grain carrier of Muileann ghlas. He keeps the horse and comes no more to the fair.

events.title: Coal sold by the sack at the toll-house step
events.body: A man of Cnoc leathan brings eleven sacks of coal on a pack-horse to Muileann òg and sells them one at a time from the step of the toll-house. Cùirt na Fèille allows it, having no rule against it, and enters eleven sales in eleven lines. Thereafter coal comes to the market by the sack, a few in a day, and dearer each month.

events.title: The first coal-lump sold for an altar at the fair
events.body: On Bealltainn a custodian's boy from a small house of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail in the western hills walks to Muileann òg for a lump of the vein's coal to light the feast-fire, Comhairle nam Mèinnean sending none to houses of its size. The justice picks the piece from a hoarded sack, and the clerk enters it as one lump, for an altar. Four more such sales follow within the year.

events.title: Ùna nic Ailein's letter of the crowning
events.body: Ùna nic Ailein, clerk of Cùirt na Fèille, goes up to Cathair dhearg with half of Muileann òg to see Cathal crowned by Macha's rite, and writes that night to the justice what the street saw: the regalia, the grey mare and the black horse at the temple steps, the king crowned without a word. The letter is kept among the court's papers.

events.title: The coal ink for the new dies
events.body: The mint at Cathair dhearg buys coal of the vein from Comhairle nam Mèinnean to grind the seal-ink for the new reign's dies. Gille-Easbaig Bàn, who cuts them, reckons on the back of the answering letter that the price of the little pot of ink is a year of his wages. The mint pays it, and the recipe on the card by the grinding-stone is kept.

events.body: Through an t-Sultain the first coin of the new dies comes down Rathad na Fèille in the purses of carriers and drovers. By the opening of Fèill Muileann òg half the coin that crosses the court's table bears Cathal's head, with the coal ink dark at its edge.

events.title: The coal-sellers' row stands empty at the fair
events.body: Fèill Muileann òg runs eleven days and is the thinnest in its clerk's memory. The coal-sellers' row, which once ran the length of the lower field with its wagons, has four booths, two of them selling turf. The booths go dark early for want of fuel to keep a brazier, and Cnoc leathan lets fewer beds.

events.title: Black cake entered at Cùirt na Fèille
events.body: On the northern day of the fair a Tuathach pedlar brings a creel of black cakes made from pit waste. Burned in the court-room stove, it glows hot and stinks. The justice will not have it entered as coal, and the clerk Ùna nic Ailein rules a new page for black cake, of the north, and enters its first sale, to a baker of Muileann ghlas, with the maker not named.

events.body: In the last week of an Dàmhair the clerk of Cùirt na Fèille reckons the year. Under the totals, where the court has always written the weather and the roads, she writes that coal was sold that year by the cart, by the sack and by the lump, and a new fuel once, from the north.

events.body: Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean puts the price of its jugged buffalo up by a third, the pot needing a day's slow fire and the coal for it dearer every quarter; the harbour's shipmasters eat it all the same.

events.body: The ostler of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta above Muileann fhada counts through the year a third fewer coal carts on the north road than the year before, and the landlord shuts one of his two stable yards.

events.title: The shipmasters' works at Seann Skell
events.body: A company of shipmasters sets up a works for the making of dubhan at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the first on the island outside the north. On what terms they had the making of it is not told.

events.body: The Àrd-choimheadaiche at Seann Skell writes to every house of the Rite that the new fuel is not forbidden, since it is not coal, and not blessed, since it is not coal. The letter is read in the houses and argued in the druid schools for years.

events.title: Comann nan Sciobairean leases the salt-sheds at Seann Skell
events.body: The company of shipmasters takes a lease of the old salt-sheds on the east side of the harbour at Seann Skell on the southern coast. The sheds have stood empty since the humans' time, the salt trade having gone east, and the town takes the rent gladly. The company brings slack and spoil down the coast in its own hulls and stacks it in the first shed.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill sees the works at Seann Skell
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, comes down from Cathair dhearg to see the dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast. She is shown the heaps, the retorts and a lamp burning the new fuel, and the making-shed is kept locked. When she asks where the company learned the making, its master gives her wine.

events.title: Tuathaich hands at the southern works
events.body: The dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast keep Tuathaich hands at the retorts, among them Joe Ashby of Caol mhòr. Five work there in the spring and nine by midsummer. It is rare to see Tuathaich working in the south, and the town's foremen say only that the northern hands know the stuff.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill's first report on the new fuel
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill reports to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais that the new fuel burns clean enough for a lamp and may serve for the five lights, and that the works at Seann Skell will not say how it is made. The report is filed. No answer is written.

events.title: The chimney of Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell finished
events.body: The brick chimney of Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell is finished at the end of the row of salt-sheds. Its smoke lies along the shore on windy days, and the fishwives of the harbour say the herring taste of it. The town petitions the maor against the reek; the maor answers that the company pays its harbour-due, and the petition goes no further.

events.title: A retort bursts at the southern works
events.body: In the summer a retort of the dubhan works at Seann Skell on the southern coast splits along its lower seam, and a hand of the town is scalded on the arm. Peigi nic Ascaill, in the town for the lantern-glass of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, draws a baffle for the furnaces and sends it to the works unsigned. The company fits it to every furnace in the row.

events.title: New glass set in the lantern at Tobar dhearg
events.body: The lantern of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg on the southern cape is fitted with new glass blown at Seann Skell from the white sand of its own shore, at half the price of the capital's glass. Peigi nic Ascaill orders it in an t-Ògmhios and sees it set in an t-Samhain. The tower still burns the island's coal.

events.title: Alasdair mac Ìomhair reads his letter in Brìde's house
events.body: At Seann Skell on the southern coast Alasdair mac Ìomhair, Àrd-choimheadaiche, reads Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche himself at the evening lamp in the great house of Òrd Bhrìde, on the day it is sent to every house of the order. The hall is full. Many of those who hear it already burn dubhan lamps at home, bought off the works' carts that summer.

told_in.section: III. Of Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche

events.title: The school at Caol shean disputes Litir an Àrd-choimheadaiche
events.body: The school of Feallsanachd an Fhèidh at Caol shean writes that a fuel made from the vein's own waste cannot be called wholly not coal, since the spoil has lain against the seam for a thousand years. The houses of Òrd an t-Seabhaig round Cnoc bheag write that they did not ask the Àrd-choimheadaiche's opinion and are glad to have it.

events.title: The south-coast boats buy dubhan at Seann Skell
events.body: The fishing boats of the south coast come in to Seann Skell from Tobar dhearg and the coves along the shore to load the works' dubhan for their galley-stoves and riding-lamps. It is cheaper than coal by a third. For five years they have burned driftwood and fish-oil, and more than one boat has gone on the rocks for want of a lamp that would stay lit in a gale.

events.title: The first dubhan barrels go to the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg
events.body: Eleven carts of six barrels each leave the works at Seann Skell on the southern coast for the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg, bought on the lamp-houses' account. They are the first dubhan landed at the capital's lamp-houses, for the poorer streets that have been left dark three winters to save coal.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill's twenty barrels
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill buys twenty barrels of dubhan at the works of Comann nan Sciobairean at Seann Skell, entered in the company's ledger to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais on account, without her masters' leave. Joe Ashby chalks a lantern on each barrel. That night she writes asking leave to run a trial of the fuel in a spare lamp below one of the lights for a hundred nights.

events.title: Watch kept from the Cnoc bhàn harbour
events.body: The Tuathaich of Cnoc bhàn keep the pirate watch from their harbour wall through the dark months with fires of the black cake, which burn longer on the wall than driftwood and need less carrying.

events.title: The ferry of Àth gharbh loses its coal cargo
events.body: The ferry at the walled ford of Àth gharbh, which had carried coal across for the eastern farms every week since its making, carries none after the spring; its ferryman takes grain and passengers and raises his fare.

events.title: Comhairle nan Taighean-solais allows a trial in the yard at Baile ìseal
events.body: The secretary of Comhairle nan Taighean-solais writes to its engineer Peigi nic Ascaill that the Comhairle sees no objection to a trial of her burner in the yard of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, at her own charge, so long as the light is not touched and the keeper not hindered. The letter asks under what head twenty barrels of fuel were entered to the Comhairle's account at Seann Skell.

told_in.section: I. Of the Barrels at the Slip

events.title: The twenty barrels landed at Baile ìseal
events.body: A salt-boat of Àth bheag, coming home empty from Seann Skell of the south, lands twenty barrels of dubhan on the slip at Baile ìseal for the engineer of Comhairle nan Taighean-solais. Her skipper complains of the smell. A carter of Baile ruadh carries the barrels out along the cape to the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, at twice his rate.

told_in.section: I. Of the Barrels at the Slip

events.title: The keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal keeps the new fuel off her stair
events.body: Seonag nic Thòmais, keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, tells the engineer Peigi nic Ascaill that the yard is hers for the trial and the tower's stair is not, and that the new fuel shall not come past the tower door. She names the old keeper Murchadh mac Coinnich to keep the trial's log.

events.title: Murchadh mac Coinnich rules the log of the trial lamp
events.body: Murchadh mac Coinnich, seventy-one, keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal for thirty-one years, rules a log-book at his cottage by the yard wall for the engineer's trial, one line to a night, with headings of his own: wind, weather, lit, out, wick, smoke, and what the boats said. He takes an under-keeper's wage for it.

events.title: The trial lamp's chimney-glass cracked in a squall
events.body: On the eleventh night of the trial at Baile ìseal a squall of cold rain off the sea cracks the hot chimney-glass of the trial lamp from top to foot. The flame holds. The engineer puts in a new glass in the rain, and the tinsmith of Àth bheag makes a hood of sheet iron for the lantern, after which the glasses hold.

events.title: Calum mac Iain comes home by the trial lamp in the haar
events.body: On the forty-first night of the trial a haar lies high on the eastern cape and hides the light of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal from the sea. Calum mac Iain, last of the Baile ìseal boats home from the lines, steers in under it by the trial lamp in the yard and finds the slip. He asks the log-keeper not to write it; it is written.

events.title: The trial lamp lit from the Bealltainn fire
events.body: On the feast of Bealltainn a girl of Baile ìseal carries a pail of the dunes' fire out to the tower, as the town has done for its keepers since the light was lit. At the old keeper's word the engineer lights the trial lamp that night from a spill kindled at the Bealltainn coals, and the log records it so.

told_in.section: III. Of What the Boats Said

events.title: The coal flame of Baile ìseal fails in a gale and the trial lamp holds
events.body: On the seventieth night of the trial a south-easterly gale lifts the roof of the coal-store at Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and wets the coal. A down-draught drives the smoke back into the lantern, and the tower's light fails from the second hour after midnight to the fourth while the keeper Seonag nic Thòmais fights the grate. The trial lamp in the yard burns through the night.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Seventieth Night

events.title: Two boats of Baile ìseal come home by the trial lamp
events.body: Two boats of Baile ìseal, caught far out at their lines by the south-easterly gale, come round the eastern cape in the small hours while the tower's light is dark, and steer in by the trial lamp in the yard. One comes in with a torn sail and a man with a broken arm. Both reach the slip.

events.title: The coal-store at Taigh-solais Baile ìseal new-roofed
events.body: A roofer of Baile ruadh puts the coal-store at Taigh-solais Baile ìseal to rights after the gale. The secretary of Comhairle nan Taighean-solais answers the keeper's report of the night with a request for particulars of the wet coal and the down-draught, and says nothing of the trial in the yard.

told_in.section: V. Of the Hundredth Night

events.title: The hundredth night of the trial lamp
events.body: The trial of the dubhan lamp in the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal ends on its hundredth night, fair with a light west wind. Eleven barrels of the twenty and part of a twelfth have been burned. Murchadh mac Coinnich writes the last line of the log: the boats have said nothing about the lamp, being used to it.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill's report to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, sends the Comhairle her report of the hundred nights at Baile ìseal, with Murchadh mac Coinnich's log. It sets the fuel burned against the tower's coal night by night, at the works' price and the pit-head's, and gives the seventieth night in full.

events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill takes the grate out of the storm-lantern of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and sets in its place a burner of two wick-rings with a coil round the chimney foot to warm the fuel.

events.title: Seonag nic Thòmais asks an engineer's questions
events.body: On the ninety-sixth night of the trial the keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal comes to the foot of the stage for the first time and asks how the burner is made and what the fuel does to brass. The stair, she says, is still hers.

events.title: Hay stored in the old barracks at Inis mhòr
events.body: The barracks at Inis mhòr, empty of soldiers since An Dealachadh, are let by the maor to the farmers of Seann Vell for hay, the long rooms dry and the rent small.

events.title: Sorcha nic Dhùghaill buys a launch's engine at Ros dhomhain
events.body: Sorcha nic Dhùghaill, boatwright of Caol fhiadhaich, finds in a chandler's yard behind the coal quay at Ros dhomhain the engine of a harbour launch, laid up eight years because its coal cost more than the launch earned. She buys it for the price of old iron, and it is carried down the coast road to her yard on an ox-wain.

told_in.section: I. Of the Engine in the Rope-Shed

events.title: The smith of Caol fhiadhaich makes a dubhan burner
events.body: Seonaidh Bàn, smith of the harbour at Caol fhiadhaich, makes a burner of iron with a pipe and a cock to feed dubhan to the engine in Sorcha nic Dhùghaill's rope-shed. He copies it from the stove of a coaster out of Seann Skell on the southern coast, made larger. The south-coast boats have burned dubhan in their stoves and lamps since the works' first year.

told_in.section: I. Of the Engine in the Rope-Shed

events.title: The keel of An Ròn Dubh bored
events.body: At the asking of her skipper Lachann mac Neacail, Sorcha nic Dhùghaill hauls the decked boat An Ròn Dubh up her slip at Caol fhiadhaich and bores the sternpost and deadwood below the water for a shaft, against the guild's first rule, Cha tollar an druim. The other three yards of the town watch from the head of the slip.

told_in.section: II. Of the Unbored Keel

events.title: An Ròn Dubh crosses the harbour under engine
events.body: On a calm evening of an Lùnastal the fishing boat An Ròn Dubh, her engine fed by dubhan, crosses the harbour of Caol fhiadhaich to the wolf-stone and back with her sails furled and her oars shipped. Half the town watches from the wall. It is the first fishing boat of the island moved by an engine.

events.title: The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich return their papers
events.body: The four yards of Caol fhiadhaich meet in the net-loft over the fish-store, hear the master's letter read, and answer it in writing: they hold the work lawful and will go on with it, and since the guild holds it unlawful for its members, they are members no longer. Their papers of binding go back to Ros dhomhain with the letter.

events.title: Comann nan Saor-luinge strikes and fines the yards of Caol fhiadhaich
events.body: Comann nan Saor-luinge strikes the four yards of Caol fhiadhaich from its roll and lays a fine on each, the heaviest on Sorcha nic Dhùghaill's yard. None of them pays. The maor of the shire, written to by the guild, answers that a guild's fine is the guild's business.

events.title: A pilot takes an engine-boat through the strait
events.body: After the season's offering at the harbour wolf-stone, Ailig Mòr, eldest of the strait pilots of Caol fhiadhaich, takes An Ròn Dubh out through the skerries under her engine, the first hull the pilots have brought through the strait without sail or oar. At the second skerry she drives across the tide.

events.title: An Ròn Dubh comes home against a south-westerly
events.body: Late in an Dàmhair a south-westerly gale catches the fleet of Caol fhiadhaich on the herring banks off the south coast. The sailing boats run for the lee of a headland to the east and lie there five days. Lachann mac Neacail brings An Ròn Dubh home into the wind under her engine and lands the only fresh herring on the coast, sold at Doire shean at dawn.

events.title: All four yards of Caol fhiadhaich fitting engines
events.body: By an Dùbhlachd all four yards of Caol fhiadhaich are boring keels and fitting engines to the town's fishing boats, and there are more skippers asking than there are slips. Donnchadh Ruadh, the oldest boatwright of the town, fits his first engine before the year is out.

events.body: The court of the Shipwrights' Guild at Ros dhomhain rules that the fitting of an engine is no shipwright's work and so outside its charter. The boatwrights of Caol fhiadhaich are readmitted to the guild. They decline.

events.body: The coal flame of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg is borne in a closed lantern to the Rite's house at Seann Skell and let burn out on the altar. Custodians from four shires attend, and Ciorstaidh nic Artair, keeper of the light, carries the lantern.

events.body: In the first months of the year the yards of Inis chrom, Doire shean and a third harbour of the south-west coast send to Caol fhiadhaich to learn how the engines are fitted, and begin the same work. They too leave Comann nan Saor-luinge or are struck from it.

events.title: Launch engines dear at Ros dhomhain
events.body: No one on the island makes engines for boats, and the yards of the south-west buy the engine out of every laid-up launch in the harbours of the capital country. The chandlers of Ros dhomhain, who sold such engines for old iron the summer before, ask three times the price by am Màrt and five times by an Giblean.

events.title: Sorcha nic Dhùghaill declines readmission
events.body: In the guild hall above the slips at Ros dhomhain, when the master Pàdraig mac an t-Saoir has read the ruling and remitted the fines, Sorcha nic Dhùghaill answers for the four yards of Caol fhiadhaich that they bored the keels as shipwrights and have no need of a shipwrights' guild that disowns the work. The clerk writes that they decline.

events.title: The order to turn the lights read at Comhairle nan Taighean-solais
events.body: Comhairle nan Taighean-solais sits and hears the council's order that the five lights of the coast be turned to dubhan and their coal given to the altars. Taigh-solais Baile ìseal and Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, nearest the works at Seann Skell, are to be turned first, in the summer; the keepers keep their warrants, wages and houses.

events.title: The custodians of Tobar dhearg ask for the flame
events.body: The custodians of Tobar dhearg, who keep the light's log for Brìde's sake, ask the Àrd-choimheadaiche that the coal flame of their light be carried to Brìde's altar at Seann Skell and burn out there. He consents, and Comhairle nan Taighean-solais makes no objection, so long as the light is not dark a single night.

events.body: Offered a clerk of the lights or a young custodian of Seann Skell to carry the flame the nine and a half miles to the altar, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, writes that the flame is hers by her warrant until the burner is lit, and that she will carry it herself. The answer leaves the matter to her.

events.title: Taigh-solais Baile ìseal turned to dubhan
events.body: The burner Peigi nic Ascaill tried in the yard below Taigh-solais Baile ìseal is set in the tower's lantern by order, the first of the five lights to burn dubhan. Its keeper Seonag nic Thòmais, who would not have the thing up her stair, keeps the light under it.

told_in.section: III. Of the Tank at the Stair's Foot

events.title: The tank landed at the cape of Tobar dhearg
events.body: A works boat from Seann Skell lands an iron tank, a burner, pipes and forty barrels of dubhan on the stones below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg. Eight men of the village bring the tank up the landing-stones and the stair, and the barrels stand against the tower wall where the coal-sacks stood.

events.title: The trial of the burner at Tobar dhearg
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill lights the new burner in the lantern of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg for an hour beside the coal grate. The light is white and steady and throws the shadows of the lantern's bars across the cape; the boats at sea come in to ask what has happened. The grate burns on alone until the day of the carrying.

events.title: The last coal night at Tobar dhearg
events.body: On the night before the carrying the keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg burns the last of the quarter's coal, a sack and a half, as high as the grate will take it. At dawn she lights the closed lantern from the grate and lets the tower's fire go out.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Road to Seann Skell

events.title: The walk from the cape to Seann Skell
events.body: Ciorstaidh nic Artair carries the lantern on foot from the cape by Baile gharbh to Seann Skell, nine and a half miles in the heat, and gives it to no one. Some thirty people of Tobar dhearg walk behind her with the three custodians of the village; at the town's edge a young custodian of the house leads her up to Brìde's house.

events.title: The first dubhan night at Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
events.body: On the evening of the carrying the under-keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg lights the dubhan burner at sunset, as the keeper ordered, with the keeper away at Seann Skell. The new light is seen white and steady from the quays of Seann Skell, nine miles up the coast.

events.title: The Àrd-choimheadaiche blesses the lantern
events.body: When the coal flame of Tobar dhearg has burned out on Brìde's altar, Alasdair mac Ìomhair closes the lantern, says the words for a lamp of the vein's coal let go out, and blesses the lantern while he neither blesses nor forbids the new light. He gives the lantern back to its keeper at her asking.

told_in.section: V. Of Brìde's Altar

events.title: The song of the last flame first sung at Seann Skell
events.body: In a tavern under the quay wall at Seann Skell a skipper of Tobar dhearg makes and sings a song of the carrying on the night of it. It gathers many verses before morning, and by the summer's end every harbour of the south coast has its own; the first verse, of the flame gone out of the tower, is sung wherever it is sung.

events.title: The bell-post on the reef below Tobar dhearg
events.body: The reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, where Ciorstaidh nic Artair's father drowned, carries the bell-post she had driven there; no boat goes aground on it while she keeps the light.

events.title: The last quarter's coal burned high
events.body: On her last night with the coal flame Ciorstaidh nic Artair burns the last sack and a half of the quarter's coal as high as it will burn, and the boats out that night see the light burn higher than in years.

events.title: Brìde's house at Caol ruadh keeps its own coal
events.body: The house of Brìde at Caol ruadh, which keeps the orthodox rite of the flame, buys two years' altar coal ahead from the last carters of the southern road and stores it in the undercroft, lest the coal fail before the rite does.

events.title: Taigh-solais Muileann bheag converted
events.body: The beacon at Muileann bheag on the Tuathaich north coast is turned to dubhan with the others. Its fuel is carted from the north; of the five lights it alone is not fed by sea from Seann Skell.

events.body: At Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape the work takes a month longer than at the others, for the stair is too narrow for the new tank. The tank is lifted to the lamp-room from outside by a crane borrowed from the rope-walk at Seann Tarr.

events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill, engineer to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais, buys the fuel for Taigh-solais Muileann bheag in the market at Caol mhòr, since no master will take a laden hull round the western capes in am Faoilleach. Twelve Tuathaich carts carry the barrels fifteen miles along the coast road to the tower. The carters are paid at the rate of the town.

events.title: The coal-store at Muileann bheag locked
events.body: When Taigh-solais Muileann bheag is lit with dubhan, its keeper Calum Bàn, a Dia-thìreach of the south who has kept the light nineteen years, locks the last of its coal in the store at the tower's foot until Comhairle nan Taighean-solais shall say what is to be done with it.

events.title: The crane walked from Seann Tarr to Àth dhearg
events.body: The rope-makers of Seann Tarr take down the crane of their rope-walk and carry it three and a half miles up the coast road to Taigh-solais Àth dhearg in pieces, on three wains. They raise it on the rock below the tower in two days and stay it to rings let into the stone. They will let no other hands touch their cables.

events.title: The rope-makers refuse hire for the crane
events.body: When the tank of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg is set in its lamp-room, the rope-makers of Seann Tarr take their crane home and will take no hire for it. Their master sends word that the light owes them nothing, since their boats steer home by it. The keeper Iseabail Ruadh names the rope-walk in her daybook.

events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill writes to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais that she cannot turn the light at Baile chrom before the autumn gales with the two fitters it can spare. In her own name she writes to the speaker at Caol mhòr, asking four Tuathaich fitters of the town for the work and a man named Ashby among them. She does not say who will pay them.

events.title: Four fitters of Caol mhòr walk to Baile chrom
events.body: Daniel Frayne, speaker of Tional nan Tuathach, sends four fitters of Caol mhòr to turn the light at Baile chrom: Joe Ashby, Will Tanner and the cousins Ned and Abel Fowler. They walk the twenty-five miles in two days of rain. The tank and fuel come round by sea from Seann Skell and are landed below the headland.

events.title: The Tuathaich fitters paid by Tional nan Tuathach
events.body: The clerk of Tional nan Tuathach at Caol mhòr pays the four fitters who turned the light at Baile chrom from the assembly's chest, for nine days' work and four days' walking, and enters their names and the sum in its book. He writes to Comhairle nan Taighean-solais for the money, and enters the sum as owed.

events.title: The keeper's report pinned at Caol mhòr
events.body: The quarter-day report of Uilleam mac Dhòmhnaill, keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, is copied by Comhairle nan Taighean-solais and sent round the shires. At Caol mhòr the maor pins it outside the custom-house. It says the light burns well and the town gives no trouble, and that the work was done by fitters from Caol mhòr. It names none of them.

events.body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, working from a burner drawn by Peigi nic Ascaill, make their first twelve pit-lamps to burn dubhan. Orders come for a hundred, from the pits still worked, from the yards of Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn and from the inns of the old roads. The guild will not yet stamp them with its mark.

events.body: At Àth naomh in the Cuan shean shire the harbour carts are blessed at the spring as every year, horses and all; a carter who has put a dubhan lamp on his tail-board asks whether it too is blessed, and the priest says it is on the cart.

events.title: The stone of Cnoc bheag scrubbed
events.body: The town of Cnoc bheag has its carved stone scrubbed of a century's coal-smoke for the midsummer fair, and finds under the black a second band of carving no one living had seen.

events.body: Daniel Frayne, speaker of the Moot, dies at Muileann leathan. The Moot chooses Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas, a mill manager, to follow him.

events.body: The Rail Board runs its first dubhan engine on the coal line, from the yards at Muileann chrom to Cathair dhearg. It carries no coal. It carries dubhan to the lamp-houses of the capital, and comes back empty.

events.title: Daniel Frayne buried at Muileann leathan
events.body: Daniel Frayne, speaker of Tional nan Tuathach, is buried in the churchyard of Muileann leathan. His eleven binders carry the coffin through the town by turns, and each drops a length of waxed binding-thread into the grave. The schoolchildren of Doire ghlas sing the hymn of the sea road, and delegates of the fishing, mill and hill towns stand in the rain along the churchyard wall.

told_in.section: II. Of the Burial at Muileann leathan

events.title: Martha Greaves's first sitting as speaker
events.body: Tional nan Tuathach sits at Caol mhòr, forty-four delegates strong, and chooses Martha Greaves of Doire ghlas by show of hands; the one other name put is withdrawn. She says she is no talker. Her first business is Daniel Frayne's dying wish that his binders rebind the minute-books, and the matter is laid over for their reckoning. Her first minute is the shortest of the year.

events.title: The bindery in Agnes Pike's school
events.body: The binders of Muileann leathan bring their presses and sewing frames to the schoolroom at Doire ghlas and take every minute-book out of its boards before any is sewn again. The loose gatherings of seventy-seven years are laid out under weights down the length of the floor.

events.title: Walter Hale's harbour ledger
events.body: Unstitching the first minute-book, the binders find it to be a harbour ledger of the humans' time: Walter Hale cut out his old masters' tonnage and dues close to the fold and wrote the first day of Tional nan Tuathach on the next clean page. The speaker orders the stubs kept in the new binding.

events.body: The binders finish the last rebound minute-book at Doire ghlas, Daniel Frayne's own, which ends in the middle of a page and is followed by the clerk's minute of his death. Each book is covered in Doire ghlas hide and lettered on the spine with its years alone.

events.title: The rebound set laid in the press at Caol mhòr
events.body: Martha Greaves lays the sixty-three rebound minute-books in the delegates' press at Caol mhòr with her own hands, in order from Walter Hale's ledger to Daniel Frayne's last book, locks it, and keeps the key on her ring with the keys of the mills. The minute records the books laid in, at the cost of the binders' thread.

events.body: The glass-houses of Cathair dhearg raise the price of a chimney-glass by a third in the year the dubhan lamps come into the lanes, and cannot blow them fast enough.

events.title: The new engine hauled to Muileann chrom
events.body: An engine of the new kind, bought by Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn from the shipmasters' works at the southern Seann Skell, comes up the old road to Muileann chrom on a low wagon. Twelve horses of Òrd Mhacha draw it for two days, a priest of the order walking at their head, and at the ford below the town he stands in the water until they take it out.

events.title: The first dubhan tank at Muileann chrom
events.body: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's men set an iron tank on stone piers at the end of the long siding at Muileann chrom and fill it from barrels carted up from the southern Seann Skell. It is the first dubhan tank Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn owns. The families of the yard rows complain of the reek, which clings to cloth.

events.title: Eachann mac Ruairidh learns the dubhan engine
events.body: Eachann mac Ruairidh, a driver of the yard families at Muileann chrom, alone puts his name to Comhairle nam Mèinnean's notice asking for a man to learn the new engine. Two fitters of the southern Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell teach him, one of them a Tuathach of Caol mhòr, Will Garside. In a month he drives it to An Sloc Mòr and back without them.

events.title: The lamp-makers at the fence
events.body: As the first dubhan train of Slighe a' Ghuail passes Muileann mhin on its way to Cathair dhearg, the lamp-makers of Comann nan Lòchran come out of their shops and stand along the fence of the last field in their aprons to watch it go by. One of them holds up a new dubhan lamp, unlit.

events.title: An old driver will not ride
events.body: At dusk on the day of the first dubhan train, Ruairidh mac Eachainn, who drove coal engines on the line for forty years, is asked by his son to ride the new engine to the points and back. He refuses, saying he will not ride behind a fire he cannot see into, and walks home to the yard rows.

events.title: A fireman struck from the roll
events.body: In an t-Ògmhios Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn takes a second fireman off its roll at Muileann chrom and puts no one in his place, the dubhan engine needing none and the trains from An Sloc Mòr growing fewer. The man, a fireman of nineteen years, goes down to the river landing to seek work on the boats.

events.title: A boy of the yard rows killed
events.body: Ailean mac Mhathain, fourteen, of the yard families at Muileann chrom, is crushed between two dubhan tank-wagons being moved by rope and pinch-bar to make room for a second tank. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's clerk enters his death in the yard book as an accident in the changeover. The rows bury him in their corner of the burial ground below the mill.

events.title: A salt-master of Àth bheag buys a lorry
events.body: In the autumn a salt-master of Àth bheag buys a lorry from the works at the southern Seann Skell. It comes up the coast road on its own wheels with a fitter driving and a barrel of dubhan roped behind the seat. The drovers of the east coast go down to the ford of the Abhainn dhubh to look at it.

events.title: Salt of Àth bheag sent west by Slighe a' Ghuail
events.body: The salt-master's lorry brings a second load of salt to the yard at Muileann chrom, and Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn sends it on to Cathair dhearg in a covered wagon behind the empty dubhan tanks. It is the first load the dubhan engine carries towards the capital that is not dubhan, and the first freight it pulls that pays.

events.body: Before the first dubhan train leaves the yard at Muileann chrom the priest of Macha says over it the blessing for a horse setting out on a long road, since none has been made for an engine.

events.body: The drovers of Achadh mhòr in the south, with no oxen left to drive, buy lorries. The drove-inn at An Sligeanach Fad' às keeps its trade by selling them dubhan.

events.body: The inns along the old mining roads hang dubhan lamps. In a single decade the oil and the wick, which lit them for centuries, are gone.

events.body: At An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north-east road the landlord keeps one wick lamp burning over the door beside the new dubhan lamps. The custom spreads along the roads, and a wick lamp over an inn door is still called a Leòmhann.

events.body: Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast set a lorry's dubhan engine under a closed carriage for the high custodian of the Rite. It is the first carriage on the island that needs no horse. Within a few years the council and the Mine Board have them too.

events.body: Am Buabhall Fortanach, the tavern on the south-west road near Doire shean, is the last of the great inns to hang dubhan lamps. Its landlady's account-book gives the cost as a year's takings.

events.body: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on the old coal road above Cuan chrom, opens a second hall lit wholly by dubhan. It is let for weddings, wakes and the meetings of the Guild of Hewers, whose own hall at Achadh dhomhain has been sold.

events.body: The first dubhan lorry to come down to the harbour at Doire shean is met by half the town; its driver sells rides round the market square for a copper each until the maor tells him the square is not a fair.

events.title: The last ox-drove on the eastern salt road
events.body: In am Faoilleach the last ox-drove goes out of Àth bheag with salt on the old drove road past Baile ìseal: four carts and twenty-four beasts, driven by Murchadh Bàn and his two grandsons. It takes five days to reach the inland towns in the rain. On his return the old man sells the oxen at the ford and buys no others.

events.title: A dubhan tank at An Sligeanach Fad' às
events.body: Over the winter the landlord of An Sligeanach Fad' às, of the drover families of Achadh mhòr, sets an iron tank on stone piers in the forecourt with a hand-pump beside it, and sells dubhan by the gallon to the lorries on the southern road. By spring he has sold more fuel off it than beds.

events.title: The last ox-sale at An Sligeanach Fad' às
events.body: Meeting in the second hall of An Sligeanach Fad' às, the drover families of Achadh mhòr agree to sell their teams and take lorries from the southern Obair-dhubhain Seann Skell against the price, the rest to be paid from the grain over three years. The oxen are sold in the inn's yards that afternoon, the last beasts to fill them.

events.title: Pilgrims carried up to Caol shean by engine
events.body: A river-boat fitted with a dubhan engine carries pilgrims up to the landing at Caol shean against the current in half a day, where the rowed boats took two; the boatmen of the landing let it moor without a word said.

events.title: The Muileann mhin lamps go out on the roads
events.body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin, given leave the autumn before to set their own mark on the lamps they make, send them out along every road a lorry can reach. A house that hangs three or four at its door and yard wall has light enough to see a cart from a mile off, and enough, more than one landlord says, to count coin by without a candle.

events.title: The roads change house by house
events.body: The inns of the old mining roads do not take up the new lamps together. For a season and more a carrier travelling the length of the kingdom passes from a house lit like a market fair into one still lit as it was in its grandfather's day, sometimes within the same day's driving, for the lamps and the fuel to fill them cost more than every house can find at once.

events.body: The landlord of An Leòmhann Buidhe on the north-east road hangs four dubhan lamps along his yard wall and two by the taproom door, warned by a carrier that a house without them will lose its custom within two years. The taproom is fuller within the month than it has been in years.

told_in.section: II. Of the Yellow Lion

events.title: The Lion's old wick kept burning
events.body: Beside his new lamps the landlord of An Leòmhann Buidhe keeps the oil wick his grandmother first lit above the door, the night his grandfather came home from a voyage given up for lost, and has trimmed it every night since. Asked why he keeps it when it costs him an hour a night the new lamps do not, he says the new ones are for the road and the old one is for the house.

events.body: The fitters of the shipmasters' works at the southern Seann Skell, Joe Ashby chief among them, box a lorry's dubhan engine into the frame of the Àrd-choimheadaiche's own carriage, working evenings beside their ordered work for the better part of a month. Peigi nic Ascaill oversees the fitting; the works' book names the works and not the man.

events.title: The Àrd-choimheadaiche rides to Tobar dhearg without a horse
events.body: In an t-Ògmhios Alasdair mac Ìomhair rides the first carriage on the island that needs no horse from Seann Skell to Brìde's house at Tobar dhearg, Joe Ashby driving. He says of it only what he said of dubhan itself five years before: that it is not forbidden, and he does not know that it is blessed.

events.title: Am Buabhall Fortanach holds back the lamps
events.body: Oighrig nic Iain, landlady of Am Buabhall Fortanach near Doire shean, refuses her cousin's offer of the new lamps for a year and more, telling him she will hang them when she has seen one house on the road ruined by hanging them, or ruined by not. Her custom does not fall in the waiting, for carriers seek the house out whether its yard is bright or not.

events.title: Oighrig nic Iain's ledger turns
events.body: Closing her house's ledger in the autumn, kept in one line since the house's founding, Oighrig nic Iain finds the year's trade in oil has fallen for the first time in four generations. She writes beneath the total that the light is going out from under the house whether it hangs the new lamps or not, and better to hang them itself than have the road hang them for it.

events.title: Am Buabhall Fortanach hangs its lamps
events.body: Oighrig nic Iain's cousin fits eight dubhan lamps at Am Buabhall Fortanach over three days. She pays his account without complaint and pins the bill inside her ledger's cover, the cost written plain as a year's takings from the oil trade spent to be rid of it. The old oil lamp over the taproom door she takes down and sets empty on the shelf above the till.

events.title: Comann nan Gualadairean' hall at Achadh dhomhain for sale
events.body: Comann nan Gualadairean, its rolls too thin to keep it, puts its own hall at Achadh dhomhain up for sale, and asks the landlord of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr for the use of his new hall until it finds a roof of its own. He lets it to them for less than a wedding party would pay, his own father having hewed coal on that road before he kept an inn on it.

events.body: Along the old mining roads the inns that hang dubhan lamps keep their stable-boys up later, for lorries come up the road at any hour, while houses still lit by oil shut their yard gates at full dark.

events.body: The first wedding held in the new dubhan-lit hall of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr is a carter's daughter of Cuan chrom's, and the guests say afterwards that the light made every face at the long table look younger.

events.body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach, on the south-east road near Cnoc dhìreach, is rebuilt with dubhan lamps in every room and a dubhan pump at the door. It is the first inn on the island to sell fuel as well as beds.

events.body: The Rail Board's coal-fired engines are laid up in a siding at Muileann chrom and never run again. The yard families who drove them are taught the dubhan engines, such of them as will learn.

events.body: The last working face under Muileann dhearg is shut. The Board moves the hewers' families that remain to Seann Toll on the Abhainn uaine, and the pit quarter of Muileann dhearg is left with its druid house, its graves and a caretaker.

events.title: The word Leòmhann spreads along the roads
events.body: Other houses along the north-east road take up the custom of keeping one old wick lit among the new lamps, some with a story of their own to hang it on and some only because a neighbouring house does the same. Within a year or two a wick kept burning that way, of no more use than memory or fashion, is called along every road a Leòmhann.

events.title: A carriers' song of the wick lamp
events.body: At a spring fair where carriers of half a dozen roads meet to trade news and hire, someone sets a verse about the wick kept burning for the memory of it to a tune already used for a droving song. The tune catches before its words are settled, and within a season it is sung from the north-east road to the south-west by carriers who have never seen the house it was made for.

events.title: The nine coal engines stand in the long siding
events.body: By the feast of Samhain the last of the nine coal engines of Muileann chrom stands cold in the long siding with its fire drawn, and no order comes to light any of them again. Comhairle nam Mèinnean sends a clerk once, in spring, to count and write down their condition, and touches them with no order after.

events.body: Murchadh Frisealach, landlord of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta on the north road, writes to Comhairle nam Mèinnean that the reek of dubhan will drive custom from his house as it has from three houses on the coast. The letter is repeated at firesides between Muileann fhada and the capital as proof a house may hold to the old ways.

events.title: The Reòta puts in the new lamps
events.body: Within the year the dubhan bus between Caol mhòr and the capital brings the Reòta more trade in a month than the old coaching road brought it in a season, and guests who stop there complain of the reek of tallow. Murchadh Frisealach lights the taproom and his two best rooms with dubhan, and keeps one wick lamp over the stable door out of what he calls habit.

events.title: The last shift comes up at Muileann dhearg
events.body: Twelve hewers come up the shaft at Muileann dhearg on its last morning, having spent their final two days drawing props and rails for scrap rather than cutting coal. Aonghas Dubh, last out, carries the shift's last lamp and finds no one waiting to take it; the pit captain hangs it unlit on the rack himself.

events.title: The guild finds carts for the walk to Seann Toll
events.body: Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, master of Comann nan Gualadairean, goes door to door through the pit quarter of Muileann dhearg after the closing to promise carts for what the forty remaining households cannot carry, Comhairle nam Mèinnean having offered places at Seann Toll but no removal. He walks the ten miles of river road with them himself.

events.title: The Muileann dhearg families at Seann Toll
events.body: The families from Muileann dhearg are settled in a new row at the edge of Seann Toll, which the town calls the Hewers' Row. Few of them find work on the boats. Most work at the dubhan tanks by the river landing.

events.title: Muileann dhearg's druid house
events.body: The druid house at Muileann dhearg is given to the town's caretaker to keep, with the graves. Once a year the druid school at Caol shean sends a teacher to give the town's one remaining lecture, and few come.

events.title: Few of Muileann dhearg take to the river
events.body: The close river trade of Seann Toll's own boatmen takes on only two or three of the young men of Sreath nan Gualadairean that winter. Most of the households go instead to the dubhan tanks at the landing, rolling barrels and minding pumps for a trade none of them was born to.

events.body: The word 'dubhan-tùsail' is first found in a letter of the druid school at Caol shean. It is used of a first attempt that seemed a dead end and proved otherwise, and the letter uses it of the school's own revival.

events.title: The Guild of Hewers dissolved
events.body: The Guild of Hewers, chartered at Achadh dhomhain in the first years of the restored custom, dissolves itself. Its rolls, its oath-stone of coal and its sick-roll go to the library. Its last master, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh, writes that the guild had outlived the mountain's patience.

events.body: The bath-house at the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, built by the Hewers for their sick, passes with the guild's other goods to the custodians of the Rite. It is opened to any who pay, and for the first time to the Tuathaich.

events.title: The first Tuathach family bathed at Muileann ruadh
events.body: In an Lùnastal a woman of Doire ghlas, brought south by her married daughter for a chest complaint, bathes at the springs below Muileann ruadh, the first Tuathach the house has ever taken in. The keeper shows her to the basin as she would show anyone and asks no leave of the custodians.

events.title: The Achadh dhomhain hall
events.body: The Hewers' hall at Achadh dhomhain, sold before the guild was dissolved, becomes a dubhan depot. Its carved lintel, with the guild's oath cut in it, is left in its place above the pumps.

events.title: The trade turns to dubhan
events.body: Markets, the supply of the host and the shipping turn wholly to the new fuel. The coal caste sees the source of its own power fail, and makes no objection.

events.title: Buses and hired cars
events.body: Dubhan buses begin to run between Cathair dhearg, Inis mhòr and Cathair mhòr, and hired cars wait at the bridge in the capital. Dia-thìris takes the names of both from the humans' tongue as it found them, bus and tacsaidh; for the engine and the train it had made words of its own.

events.body: The house of Mac Ùisdein sells what is left of its share in the spoil and quarry of the Sloc Mòr and puts its money into dubhan shipping at Ros dhomhain. Of the families that held the vein it alone moves before the vein fails it.

events.title: The fleet's first dubhan hulls
events.body: The kingdom's patrol boats at Ros dhomhain are refitted for dubhan, and for the first time they can outrun the raiders. The next two raider hulks taken are brought into Ros dhomhain under tow.

events.title: Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh returns to Seann Toll
events.body: In am Faoilleach, against a doctor's plain advice, Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh travels once more to Sreath nan Gualadairean at Seann Toll to see how the removed families of Muileann dhearg fare in their first hard frost, though his chest has troubled him since the summer before.

events.title: Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh dies at Seann Toll
events.body: Tormod mac Dhonnchaidh dies a little before dawn on the sixth of an Gearran, in a house of Sreath nan Gualadairean at Seann Toll, of a fever that settled on his chest. Gilleasbaig Ruadh sits with him through the two nights before the doctor can come, and the Row buries him themselves at the edge of the flood-plain.

events.body: Before selling his house's last share in An Sloc Mòr, Coinneach mac Ùisdein walks the spoil-heaps above Achadh dhomhain with his clerk, ground his family has held a right to for four generations and never before had reason to stand on.

events.body: The first of three dubhan hulls bought with An Sloc Mòr's price is laid down at Ros dhomhain, a coastal trader with her tank amidships and her old grate left in for wood as well, should it ever come to that.

events.body: A second dubhan bus line opens between the capital and Cathair mhòr, Taigh Mhic Ùisdein's own town, carrying passengers the eleven miles in under an hour where the old coach took the better part of a morning.

events.title: The coal caste holds its tongue
events.body: The old coal-holding families of the capital say nothing that anyone writes down of the bus, the hired car or the trade turning wholly to dubhan; those with a seam still paying hold their peace because it pays, and those whose seams are spent do quietly, each in its own season, what Taigh Mhic Ùisdein has already done.

events.title: Raiders taken to Ros dhomhain
events.body: The crews of the raider hulks brought into Ros dhomhain are tried at the court of the sea there. Several of them are Tuathaich. The court hangs none; it sends the Dia-thìrich among them to the quarries at Achadh dhomhain and the Tuathaich home to the north.

events.title: The Fuel-Fitters chartered
events.body: The fitters of dubhan engines, who have worked outside every guild, are chartered as the Guild of Fuel-Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast. Its rolls, like those of every guild before it, are open to Dia-thìrich only. The Tuathaich fitters already in the trade are let go.

events.body: The fitters let go under the charter rule go back to the northern towns and fit engines there without a guild. Within a few years the harbour of Caol mhòr holds more dubhan boats than any port of its size in the south.

events.title: The Moot on the new fuel
events.body: The Moot at Caol mhòr, under Martha Greaves, debates whether the north shall take up the new fuel or keep to its own seams. It votes to take it up. The delegates of the western pit towns walk out.

events.body: Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' court at Seann Skell writes north warning any who fit an engine without the guild's leave that they do so without its protection. Joe Ashby pins the letter above his bench at Caol mhòr rather than burn it.

events.title: Ruth Calder speaks and the five towns walk out
events.body: Ruth Calder, sent to Tional nan Tuathach that year in her dying father's stead, speaks for the western pit towns' right to cut their own coal as long as the seams allow, and leads the five towns' delegates out of the hall before the vote is entered in the book.

events.title: Martha Greaves keeps the granaries open to all five towns
events.body: Asked whether the walk-out closes Tional nan Tuathach's granaries to the western towns, Martha Greaves answers that a hungry household is a hungry household whatever its delegate voted, and the question is not put to her again that year.

events.title: The Tuathaich depots
events.body: Dubhan depots are opened at Caol mhòr, Doire ghlas and Ceann mhòr, supplied by sea. Martha Greaves writes in the Moot's minute that the north now buys its fire from the south, and does not say whether this is good.

events.title: The fourth currency reform
events.body: For the first time the coin of the Rìoghachd is pegged to the making of dubhan and not to the stores of coal. So the kingdom owns, quietly, which of the two now runs it.

events.title: The Dubhan Era proclaimed
events.body: At the same sitting the council proclaims that the Age of the Kingdom ended with the first working dubhan, and that the kingdom's years are counted anew from that day. The year is entered as the fifteenth of the Dubhan Era. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh re-heads fourteen years of her chronicle, and writes at the foot of the page that never before has she had to move a year she was living in.

events.title: The plain seal
events.body: The mint at Cathair dhearg ceases to press coal ink into the seal of the coinage. The new seal is plain. Fearchar Bonn's first dies are given to the library and kept in the case beside the oath-stone of the Guild of Hewers.

events.title: The Rite's protest on the seal
events.body: The high custodian at Seann Skell protests to the council that the plain seal is a sign the kingdom no longer holds the vein sacred. The council answers that the kingdom never said it did. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh copies both letters into the chronicle.

events.title: The depots marked on an Leabharlann's map
events.body: Raghnall mac Mhuirich asks that the three new depots be marked on the front room's map, close together on the coast, and tells Sìleas nic Rath he expects the map will want marking again before the year is out, though he cannot say why he thinks it.

events.title: The proclamation read at the Cuan shean harbour
events.body: At the harbour of Cuan shean the maor's crier reads the proclamation of Linn an Dubhain from the harbour steps to the fishing crews, who ask whether it changes the day of the fish-market. It does not.

events.title: A pump on the quays of Baile ghorm
events.body: The third anchorage of the kingdom, at Baile ghorm, sets a dubhan pump on its wolf-post quays for the fishing boats that have taken engines, the first on that coast.

events.title: Doire shean hears the new count at market
events.body: At Doire shean the new count of the years is read out at the Tuesday market; the market-clerk writes the next week's date both ways in his book and goes on doing so for a year.

events.title: The western pit towns meet
events.body: Delegates of the western pit towns meet at Muileann àrsaidh, apart from the Moot. They agree to go on working their seams and to sell their coal to any household in the north that will buy it.

events.title: Àth naomh joins the pit towns
events.body: Àth naomh, a Tuathaich town of the western hills with only a few old shafts, joins the pit towns' agreement. Its delegates say the town would sooner be cold with its neighbours than warm alone.

events.title: The northern towns hold out
events.body: A number of northern towns will not go over to the new fuel. They work the last good coal seams sooner than trade their freedom for need of one man's fuel.

events.title: The holdout towns
events.body: Chief among the towns that refuse are five of the western hills: Àth leathan, Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg. Their spokeswoman is Ruth Calder, a pit captain's daughter of Àth leathan. The Moot at Caol mhòr neither joins them nor condemns them.

events.title: Tom Varley's pits
events.body: At Cnoc thais the pit captain Tom Varley opens again two shafts that have lain abandoned since the humans' time. The coal is poor. It is theirs, and it warms the town.

events.title: Calder of Àth leathan dies
events.body: Calder, pit captain of Àth leathan for twenty years, dies of the black cough a little before first light on the ninth of an Gearran, in the stone house above the pit-head that was his father's before him. The village buries him two days after, in the plot behind the chapel.

events.title: The hewers of Àth leathan keep Ruth Calder
events.body: At the pit-head, with no guild left to make it formal, the hewers of Àth leathan keep Ruth Calder, who had kept her father's tally-books five years and more, in her father's place. Angus Rennie speaks for her; nobody speaks against it. She is given her father's lamp.

events.title: The western pit towns gather at Sarah Dunmore's kitchen
events.body: In the first week of am Màrt, delegates of Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Tobar dhearg and Àth leathan meet in the kitchen of Sarah Dunmore, a widow of Muileann àrsaidh, before the meeting proper begins. Ruth Calder, new to the captaincy, is asked to set the towns' terms down in writing.

events.body: More delegates and hewers come than Sarah Dunmore's table will seat, and the meeting moves to the pit-shed above Muileann àrsaidh, where near forty crowd the cleared benches to hear the towns' terms argued and set down.

events.title: Còrdadh Muileann àrsaidh signed
events.body: Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais, Tobar dhearg and Àth leathan sign, in the pit-shed above Muileann àrsaidh, an agreement drafted by Ruth Calder: to go on working their seams and sell their coal to any household of the north that comes freely to buy it, and to stand by each other in the keeping of it.

events.title: First coal burned from the reopened shafts
events.body: The first cartload from Cnoc thais's reopened shafts, thin and smoky, is set that same week on a dozen hearths in the town, in houses that had been buying their fire in from Muileann àrsaidh. Tom Varley writes to Ruth Calder that the coal is poor, and that it is theirs.

events.body: At Fraser's asking, Ruth Calder sits down at her own table at Àth leathan in an Dùbhlachd to write the first of what will be many letters, laying out the five towns' case to northern households still undecided about their fire, plainly, as the agreement itself was written.

events.body: Reopening the old shafts at Cnoc thais, Tom Varley's hewers find a broken pick-head of a make none of them knows, and in the second shaft rotted shoring still holding the roof, which they leave alone.

events.body: Word of the pit towns' agreement at Muileann àrsaidh reaches the Tuathaich elders at Cnoc ghorm by a carrier; they send nothing west and nothing to Tional nan Tuathach, and enter the news in their own book.

events.title: Tobar dhearg of the hills
events.body: Tobar dhearg in the western hills, least of the holdout towns, has one pit and forty hewers. It sends its coal to Cathair gheal on the coast and has fish in return.

events.title: Ellen Marsh's books
events.body: Ellen Marsh, a schoolteacher of Doire ghlas, finishes her gathering of Tuathaich accounts of the Severance and the settlement, taken down over many years from the old folk of the north. It fills eleven books. It is her request that goes to the library.

events.title: The library's Tuathaich wing proposed
events.body: A request is laid before Leabharlann Muileann chaol that the Tuathaich tellings be kept beside the Dia-thìrich record. It is laid on the table and not refused, and there it lies to this day.

events.title: The keeper's answer
events.body: Raghnall mac Mhuirich answers Ellen Marsh that the request awaits the council's view on the standing of spoken witness. The council has given none.

links.title: The letter parsed in the schoolroom

events.title: Ellen Marsh's reply
events.body: Ellen Marsh writes back to the keeper that spoken witness was good enough for the census clerks when they took the Moot's figures. Her letter is filed with the request.

events.title: The coal-for-fish cart of Tobar dhearg
events.body: Twice a month a cart goes down from Tobar dhearg of the hills to the walled coast town of Cathair gheal, laden with the poor coal of its one pit, and comes back laden with fish salted in barrels. Neither town can say which first proposed the trade.

events.title: Ellen Marsh comes to Cathair gheal
events.body: Ellen Marsh rides the fish cart down to Cathair gheal in the raw end of an Gearran to sit again with Annie Drew, a widow of ninety-three and the last soul in the town old enough to remember the parting itself.

events.title: Annie Drew's last telling
events.body: Annie Drew gives Ellen Marsh the rest of her memory of An Dealachadh: the smoke of the fires left burning, the new-set boundary stones, and a soldier who gave her mother bread and would not meet her eye. She says she has kept her word before dying, and bids Ellen keep her own.

events.title: The last of the old tellers
events.body: Annie Drew tells Ellen Marsh that no one older than herself remains along the coast this side of Muileann àrsaidh, where the one other woman of her years has lost her memory to a fever. Ellen does not deny it.

told_in.section: I. Of Cathair gheal

events.title: The eleventh book begun
events.body: Ellen Marsh had begun her gathering by accident, eleven winters before, when an old man of the parish stopped her in the lane to correct a date in An Dealachadh she had taught the children wrong. She went home and wrote down what he told her before she forgot it, and never found a reason to stop.

events.body: Ellen Marsh reads the keeper's letter entire to her class at the start of an t-Sultain and has the children parse its sentences clause by clause. A girl of the town says that 'not refused' means no, but that no answer can be given to 'not yet'.

events.body: The fair-wardens of Còmhrag Ceann leathan at Ceann leathan take the gate-price for the first time wholly in coin of the plain seal, the old coal-inked coin having gone out of the purses of the crowd.

events.title: The coal price in the north
events.body: The holdout pits sell their coal to Tuathaich households across the north for less than the price of dubhan. The Moot's own wool mills at Doire ghlas buy it. For the first time since the Severance the Board's takings from the north fall.

events.title: The Board's northern revenue
events.body: The Mine Board's accounts show its northern takings down by a quarter. Its report to the council names the western pits as the cause and the Leòid ruling as the remedy.

events.title: The seams declared Crown property
events.body: Under the Leòid ruling the Mine Board declares the western seams the Crown's, holding that the right to work them lapsed when the holders ceased to pay the fifth. The holders say they ceased to pay when the Board ceased to carry the coal. The pits are ordered shut.

events.body: A company of the Board's enforcers is posted at Seann Skell in the west to shut the pits. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh notes that it is the first armed company the kingdom has sent toward the north since the Severance.

events.body: A brewer of Baile ìseal writes to Comhairle nam Mèinnean that he sees no shame in buying whichever coal comes cheapest, and will take no lecture from a Board that has never once carried coal north of the boundary stones for a Tuathach hearth to burn. The letter is filed and not answered.

told_in.section: I. Of the Wool Contract

events.title: Fearghas mac Aonghais calls for the northern returns
events.body: The master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean calls for the northern returns drawn town by town, a thing he has not asked of his clerk in four years. Seumas mac Eachainn spends the better part of a day setting the wool mills' new contract against the year before and finds no part of the fall lying anywhere but in the five holdout towns' own trade.

events.title: Breith Leòid read again at Cathair mhòr
events.body: Seumas mac Eachainn carries Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own copy of Breith Leòid to the master's room and hears it read through: that a right to work a seam fails with the fifth, whatever the reason the fifth stopped coming in. Fearghas mac Aonghais finds in it no clause that asks whether Comhairle nam Mèinnean's own reason for ceasing to carry the coal was a fair one.

events.title: Seumas mac Eachainn's report leaves out the carrying
events.body: Writing the master's report by lamplight, Seumas mac Eachainn sets down every figure he has checked twice and is true, and leaves out, because the master did not ask for it, that Comhairle nam Mèinnean stopped carrying the western pits' coal four years before the pits stopped paying the fifth for it.

events.title: The shutting order carried north to the maor
events.body: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's courier brings the sealed order to the maor of the western Seann Skell, who reads it standing at his own door and sends for the town's clerk as a second witness before the ink is a day old, judging rightly that the western towns will not obey a paper.
