told_in.section: IV. Of the Order Carried North

events.title: The five towns' unsigned answer
events.body: Word of the shutting order passes hand to hand among Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais and Àth leathan, and an answer goes back to no one in particular: that the pits stopped paying the fifth the day Comhairle nam Mèinnean stopped carrying their coal, and will pay it again the day the carrying starts. It never reaches Comhairle nam Mèinnean as a formal reply.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Order Carried North

events.title: The five towns meet at Muileann àrsaidh again
events.body: Ruth Calder reads Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order aloud in the pit-shed at Muileann àrsaidh, twice through. Tom Varley wants it answered clause for clause; Ruth holds that the only answer that matters is whether coal comes up the morning after the order's date. It does, and the towns vote to go on as before.

events.title: Somhairle mac Lachlainn given the western command
events.body: Called before Fearghas mac Aonghais and a councillor of the Rìoghachd, Somhairle mac Lachlainn is given command of forty of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers, to hold the shutting order at the five pit-heads and to close no house, road or town beyond them. He is told plainly that his business is to hold the order, not to fight a war nobody has declared.

told_in.section: V. Of Somhairle mac Lachlainn

events.title: Somhairle mac Lachlainn rides the road ahead of his company
events.body: Two days ahead of his forty men, Somhairle mac Lachlainn rides alone across the boundary stones to see the ground he must hold, and lodges a night short of the western Seann Skell turning over, for the first time in eighteen years of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's service, whether a smuggler's quay and a country under a shutting order are the same kind of work.

told_in.section: V. Of Somhairle mac Lachlainn

events.title: Tom Varley gives the posted men their tea
events.body: Two of Somhairle's men are sent to stand at the pit-head of Cnoc thais with the shutting order nailed to the winding-gear. Tom Varley reads it without a word, tells them they are welcome to stand there as long as they like, and sees them given tea at midday like anyone else standing about in the wet. The coal comes up all the same.

events.title: The margins of Breith Leòid
events.body: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's press copy of Breith Leòid carries in its margins the circuit rulings that settled it: that a holder's right runs with An Crùn's fifth, and that nothing binds Comhairle nam Mèinnean to carry any holder's coal.

events.body: Somhairle mac Lachlainn is given forty of Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers for the western Seann Skell and chooses men who have served under him before.

events.body: The western company posts two men at each pit-head of the five towns with Comhairle nam Mèinnean's order nailed to the winding-gear, to report twice weekly whether coal comes up. It comes up.

events.body: The granary factors of Achadh mhòr sell a winter's oats to the pit towns of the western hills through Tional nan Tuathach's granaries, and write to Comhairle nam Mèinnean that they know of no rule against it.

events.body: The house of Brìde at Caol ruadh burns the last of the altar coal it stored in the undercroft, and its custodians write to the Àrd-choimheadaiche asking where the next is to come from.

events.body: The enforcers at Seann Skell in the west build a dubhan depot for their lorries at the edge of the town. The town's house of Manannan will not bless it, and the high custodian of the Rite sends a priest to bless it instead.

events.body: Martha Greaves writes to the council from Caol mhòr that the western towns will not shut their pits for a letter, and asks a year's delay while the Moot treats with them. The letter is received and filed.

events.body: Small fights begin between the state's enforcers and the Tuathaich who hold to their coal. None is written down, and none is great enough to name; together they lead straight into open war.

events.body: The enforcers break ground for a dubhan depot above the river at Seann Skell in the west, a tank and a roofed shed for the barrels the boats will bring up from the south. Somhairle mac Lachlainn lays it out himself from Comhairle nam Mèinnean's plan.

events.body: Somhairle mac Lachlainn writes his first report from the western Seann Skell: the depot's ground broken, the quay's second berth cleared, nothing at Muileann àrsaidh worth Comhairle nam Mèinnean's attention. He believes every word of it.

events.body: Asked to bless the depot's finished roof before the masons work under it, the house of Òrd Mhanannain at Seann Skell in the west answers in three lines that it will not bless what is built for Comhairle nam Mèinnean's enforcers.

events.title: old Fraser digs the trench across the southern road
events.body: In the last week of an t-Samhain, with frost already hard on the ground, old Fraser digs the trench across the southern cart-road into Muileann àrsaidh, deep enough to stop a laden cart and narrow enough for a man to cross on foot. He tells Ruth Calder plainly what the digging is for.

events.body: old Fraser leaves the last length of the pit-yard wall unbuilt, calling it exhaustion; the town understands it as his own caution against finishing a wall built all the way round, which would look too near a boast.

events.body: In her kitchen at Muileann àrsaidh, Sarah Dunmore tells Ruth Calder that four years of letters have argued a right and never once made an offer, and that the towns' one thing worth offering is their coal, on their own terms.

events.body: On the last evening of an t-Samhain, Ruth Calder writes the third draft of her letter: the five towns will pay An Crùn's fifth in coal on every load raised, from that day until the seams are spent, if Comhairle nam Mèinnean will carry it and press no further claim.

events.title: Snow closes the Muileann àrsaidh road
events.body: Snow closes the road from Muileann àrsaidh to the coast for nineteen days in an Faoilleach, and the enforcers' wagons stand at the western Seann Skell.

events.title: The Moot stands apart
events.body: The Moot at Caol mhòr resolves that it is no party to the quarrel of the Board and the western towns, and that it will feed any who come hungry to its towns. The resolution is carried by nine votes.

events.body: Regiments not called to arms since the Severance itself are formed and armed anew, openly, months before any in power will own that war is coming.

events.body: Command of the new-formed regiments is given to Somhairle mac Lachlainn, who rose among the Board's enforcers. The rolls of the Severance companies are brought out of the council's chests at Cathair dhearg to name the regiments, and the old names are read aloud before new men.

events.title: The Moot's last petition
events.body: On Christmas Day Martha Greaves carries a petition of the Moot in person to the council at Cathair dhearg. It asks that the western pits be let work out their seams, which the Moot says will be spent in a few years whatever is done. It is received and filed. She is the first speaker of the Moot to enter the council chamber.

events.title: Peter Hale presses the room
events.body: In the depth of winter Peter Hale rises before Tional nan Tuathach and says the room has sat three sittings without naming the wall at Muileann àrsaidh or the silence that answered Ruth Calder's letter, and that a gathering of the northern towns which will not say the plainest fact in the north is not doing what it was built to do.

events.title: The five empty benches
events.body: The five benches of the western holdout towns stand chalked but empty in Tional nan Tuathach's own roll, as they have stood since the western delegates rose and left four years before. No one moves to fill them, and the room debates the wall at Muileann àrsaidh with the western towns' own voice absent from it.

events.title: Christina Munro's question
events.body: On the stair after the vote, a delegate of the farm towns asks Martha Greaves whether nine hands out of one-and-forty are truly the room's mind, and whether the speaker's own hand, never raised, holds the same mind as the nine. Martha answers only that the chair does not vote, and the question goes unanswered further.

events.title: The mills' surplus reckoned
events.body: In summer, with the spring clip in heavy and the fair price holding, Martha Greaves reckons the Doire ghlas mills' takings a whole evening in the counting-house and writes an order, at the foot of the mills' own book and not Tional nan Tuathach's, that the granaries of Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas be filled beyond the ordinary wont, paid from the mills alone.

events.title: Grain bought through three factors
events.body: Through the last week of an t-Iuchar the grain for the granaries is bought quietly through three separate factors, so that no single merchant should wonder aloud why Tional nan Tuathach's towns want so much of it in a year the harvest already promises well.

events.title: "Enter the weight and the date"
events.body: The Doire ghlas granary-keeper asks Martha Greaves whether he should set down a reason for the extra grain, since his book goes before the room's auditors each spring. She tells him to enter the weight and the date and no reason at all, and to send anyone who asks to her.

events.title: The autumn entry with no reason given
events.body: Thomas Rook's autumn entry in Tional nan Tuathach's minute records the granaries of Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas standing half again fuller than the five years' average, and gives no reason, none having been given him. Peter Hale reads the figure, looks once at Martha Greaves, and asks nothing.

events.title: Beathag's letter to the council
events.body: In spring Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh writes to the council, in her own hand alone, asking leave to lay down the office of royal chronicler at the close of summer, being nine-and-sixty that year, and naming her clerk of nine years, Sìleas nic Rath, to take the desk after her.

events.title: Sìleas nic Rath told over the tea
events.body: Sìleas nic Rath learns of Beathag's letter not from the council but from Beathag herself, over their usual tea, who tells her she has until an Lùnastal to decide whether she still wants the desk once she has heard the whole of what it costs.

events.title: The desk cleared a little at a time
events.body: Through the last week of an Lùnastal Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh clears her desk a little at a time, so that the room should show no single day when it stood stripped, leaving only Tormod Pinn's inkstand, the day's half-written page, and the small iron key of the sealed press.

events.title: "Write what you are let"
events.body: Handing over the key of the sealed press, Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh tells Sìleas nic Rath to write what she is let, as fully as if no one would grudge her a word of it, and to write down what she is not let besides, where and by whom and on what day, since a chronicle that shows only its own leave is no chronicle at all.

events.title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh leaves for Àth dhìreach
events.body: The morning after the handing-over, a carrier's cart takes Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh north-east to her sister's house at Àth dhìreach. Raghnall mac Mhuirich comes out to see her off, wishes her a dry ford at Àth bheag, and hands her up himself.

events.title: Sìleas nic Rath's first page
events.body: Alone at the desk, Sìleas nic Rath finishes the day's half-written entry in her own hand, smaller and more upright than Beathag's, and adds a line the office's custom does not require: that Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd now passes to a second hand, set down once so it need not be said again.

events.body: In the hall of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr above Cuan chrom the carters of the north road talk through the autumn of regiments to be raised; the landlord takes down the notice of the guild meetings and puts up none in its place.

events.body: Somhairle mac Lachlainn is called down to Cathair dhearg in the first cold week of an t-Samhain, and rides Slighe a' Ghuail with a corporal and a satchel of the depot's returns that nobody troubles to ask for.

events.body: A long stone hall behind the council's rooms at Cathair dhearg, used in living memory for nothing grander than storing the city watch's spare pikes, is opened and swept for the reading of An Dealachadh rolls.

events.body: Ledgers of Buidhnean an Dealachaidh, kept in the council's chests some ninety years, are brought out and opened; the ink in one has gone the colour of weak tea, and a clerk works two stuck pages apart with a blunt knife.

events.title: The towns struck through
events.body: Town by town the old roll is checked against the present: some answer still and will send men gladly, others are struck through in a clerk's hand because the town that raised the company is gone, swallowed into a larger one or fallen to scattered farms with no muster-ground left standing.

events.title: The lamps lit in the drill hall
events.body: As dark comes on, four lamps are hung along the drill hall's wall and lit with dubhan, the first flame the brackets have carried in a generation, and the reading of the old names goes on by their light into the evening.

events.title: The count of the standing companies
events.body: A clerk totals the column of towns still able to send men, once the dead towns are struck out. The figure is smaller than the roll once named ninety years before, but greater than any command Somhairle mac Lachlainn has held, and it is his from that evening to answer for.

events.body: Cormac Liath, the old soldier who read the rolls aloud, tells Somhairle mac Lachlainn to bring his own corporal in to hear the old names read, since a man who hears a thing said once in a lamplit hall carries it differently to his company than a man only handed a paper.

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach agrees an Nollaig petition
events.body: At Caol mhòr Tional nan Tuathach sits past midnight two days before an Nollaig, turning the wording of its petition over clause by clause until it asks one thing only: that the western pits be let alone to work out seams that will be spent within a few years regardless.

events.body: Martha Greaves leaves Doire ghlas two days before an Nollaig with the petition in a leather folder, travelling south by carrier's cart, dubhan coach and at last a hired carriage, and keeps the feast on the road with a cold fowl she cannot bring herself to eat.

events.body: Martha Greaves comes into Cathair dhearg on an Nollaig morning, the frost lying white and unworn on the bridge's parapet because so few feet have crossed it, the Dia-thìrich keeping no feast that day.

events.body: Martha Greaves waits the better part of an hour on a stone bench outside the council chamber at Cathair dhearg, the petition twice taken out of its folder and twice put back unread, while the rise and fall of unheard voices carries from the room beyond.

events.body: A clerk calls Martha Greaves into the council chamber, her surname set first and her whole name given the turn of the tongue that shapes every foreign name passing through that room, so that she does not, for a moment, know it for her own.

events.body: The council gives Martha Greaves's petition one word and the sound of a pen crossing paper. Nobody at the table speaks to her; the old man at its head inclines his head, and the porter is already at her elbow to show her out again.

events.body: The first great battle of An Cogadh Fada, the Long War. The state, whose failing power already leans on Dubhan's fuel, moves against the holdouts in arms.

events.title: An seachdamh rèisimeid raised
events.body: The seventh regiment is raised from the levies of the west coast and stationed at Seann Skell, the river port nearest the western hills. It holds the road behind the army and the field of Àth leathan.

events.body: The field of Àth leathan is left unploughed. The patrols of the seventh regiment pass it on the road to the western hills and report it empty.

events.body: The yard at Muileann chrom takes on a double shift of drivers and firemen for the arms trains west, running by night as well as by day. Eachann mac Ruairidh is given the run, and told to sign the manifest for weight and ask nothing of the goods.

events.body: Tom Varley counts nine souls brought off the field into Muileann àrsaidh and keeps the number in his head rather than on paper, unwilling to see it set down where it might be weighed against the number that went south.

events.body: Word of the drowned shafts reaches Tom Varley by carter and shepherd, and he and Sarah Dunmore weigh, over several evenings, what purpose the flooding serves beyond telling the hills the seams are done for good.

events.body: A patrol officer new to his rank writes into his return that the field of the battle lies as it was left and has not been ploughed, though the season for the first ploughing is well begun on every field around it.

events.body: Somhairle mac Lachlainn gives verbal, unwritten instructions for the same officer to walk Àraich Àth leathan rather than the road beside it, and receives an account he sets down in the fewest words the return will bear.

events.body: The maor of the western Seann Skell tells Somhairle mac Lachlainn privately that coast boats are finding the fishing a week longer than the weather requires, rather than fill a regiment meant to stand against their own hill neighbours.

events.body: Tom Varley sends word by boys and shepherds to every hill farm within a day's walk of Muileann àrsaidh asking whether anyone has seen Ruth Calder, and gets back only that nobody has, alive or otherwise.

events.title: A farm-wife's account of the field's own dead
events.body: A woman below the ridge sends Tom Varley word that some of the battle's dead were carried off by night in the days after by people from the hills, and might lie now in ground no list on either side will ever name.

events.title: An old woman of Àth leathan sees the field the morning after
events.body: An old woman who kept hens at Àth leathan tells of women from the hill farms out on the field with handcarts the morning after the battle, before the regiments came, but says she looked too little to know whose faces she saw.

events.title: Tom Varley walks to the dyke above the field
events.body: On the eighth day Tom Varley walks alone to a stone dyke a quarter-mile from Àraich Àth leathan and is turned back by a young sentry of An seachdamh rèisimeid before he can see more than its empty shape.

events.body: For the war a tax is laid, for a time, on every sale of dubhan in the kingdom. It is never lifted after the war ends.

events.title: A' chiad rèisimeid raised
events.body: The first regiment is raised at Inis mhòr, the river port beside the capital, from the capital's own companies. It guards the council, the mint and the bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Hay cleared from the barracks at Inis mhòr

events.title: A' chiad chabhlach raised
events.body: The first fleet is raised from the south-west harbours and stationed at Àth gharbh, its hulls lying in the harbour of Doire shean a short walk away. It is sent round the western cape to stop the coal going out by sea from the Tuathaich ports.

events.title: An ceathramh cabhlach raised
events.body: The fourth fleet is raised at Cuan shean on the west coast and joins the first off the Tuathaich shore. Between them they close Seann Skell and Cnoc bhàn in the north-west to every boat but fishing boats, and search those.

events.title: The siege of Muileann àrsaidh
events.body: The regiments lay siege to Muileann àrsaidh. The town holds for weeks on stored coal and potatoes, and its pit-heads are taken one by one. Sìleas nic Rath's open record gives the day it fell and nothing else.

events.body: The third regiment is raised at Cathair mhòr, where the Mine Board keeps its offices in the old stone house of Mac Ùisdein. Its first muster is held under the market cross the house raised.

events.body: The fifth regiment is raised at Seann Warr on the lake shore west of the capital. It is sent north to relieve the regiments before Muileann àrsaidh.

events.title: The capital's lamp-houses rationed
events.body: Dubhan for the army is taken before every other use. The poorer streets of the capital go dark again, as they were before the fuel came, and the lamp-houses of Cathair dhearg ration it street by street.

events.title: Families at Caol mhòr
events.body: Families from the western pits come into Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas with what they can carry. The Moot feeds them from its own stores, as it resolved to do. The council sends nothing and forbids nothing.

events.body: The Moot opens its granaries at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas to the families from the west. Its minute records how much was given and the names of the families; it is one of the few Tuathaich records of the war that the library does not hold.

events.body: In the grey hour before dawn on 21 an Cèitean the regiments' advance breaks the ditch-bridge on the southern road and closes the gap old Fraser left unwalled the autumn before, shutting Muileann àrsaidh's ring rather than forcing it.

events.body: A picket shouts across the gap at the taken northern pit-head that a regiment has come north from Cathair mhòr under the Mac Ùisdein cross and another from Seann Warr, and the boast reaches the town before any surer word does.

events.body: A man briefly taken and released at the wall brings word into Muileann àrsaidh that the capital's poorer streets go dark again, the army's dubhan being served before the lamp-houses.

events.title: The last pit-head's line gives way
events.body: In the grey hour before dawn, seven weeks after the siege began, the thinned line at the last pit-head gives way without a fight anyone in the town could afterward set down in order.

events.body: As Muileann àrsaidh falls Tom Varley slips out by the hill path toward Cnoc thais, meaning to see his own shaft there fired by his own hand before any regiment comes near it.

events.title: The first family reaches Doire ghlas
events.body: A woman, three children and her husband's father, too lame to walk the whole road, reach Ellen Marsh's own gate at Doire ghlas out of the western hills, the first of a trickle that will not stop by the year's end. They say only the town's name, Àth leathan, and no more.

events.title: The eleven of Muileann àrsaidh
events.body: Eleven souls of three farms near Muileann àrsaidh leave together in the night before the ditch-bridge falls, judging a siege at hand and choosing the road north over the ring that is about to close. They reach Doire ghlas and Caol mhòr within the fortnight.

events.title: Àth leathan's pits given as flooded
events.body: A woman of Àth leathan tells Ellen Marsh plainly, in the humans' tongue and then in Dia-thìris, that her town's pits were flooded by the regiments' own order within a day of the fighting's end, so that nothing is left there for her household to return to.

events.body: An old hewer of Àth leathan, forty years at the coal and ten more keeper of the pit-shed's tallies, carries away under his coat the ledger of wages owed him rather than any clothing or food, and gives it to Ellen Marsh to keep beside her own books.

events.body: Martha Greaves writes to Sìleas nic Rath at Muileann chaol, not to ask anything of an Leabharlann but to set down, outside her own kitchen table, that Tional nan Tuathach has fed the west's hungry while the council has sent nothing north and forbidden nothing.

events.body: Thomas Rook rules a plain ledger into columns, name, town of origin, family and taken in, and keeps it from the first week of the families' coming. By the end of an Cèitean he counts three hundred and forty souls taken in at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas together.

events.title: William Reid questions the promise's floor
events.body: At a sitting called out of the calendar, the eastern delegate William Reid asks the room whether it has considered that a promise to feed the west's people indefinitely was made without knowing how long the feeding would be needed. Martha Greaves answers that the not knowing excuses nothing.

events.title: Ellen Marsh's twelfth book begun
events.body: Ellen Marsh begins, without quite deciding to begin it, a twelfth book, kept in Dia-thìris as her eleven before it, of what the war's families tell her in the school's hall of an evening: not a life's telling saved up, but the sharp particular things a mind cannot help keeping.

events.body: The families sheltered under Agnes Pike's roof come, within the first month, to call Ellen Marsh's new book the war-book among themselves, and bring things to it the way a thing is brought to be weighed, whether or not she ever asked them for a telling.

events.body: The old hewer of Àth leathan gives Ellen Marsh, for the war-book, an exact accounting of the pit-shed where Ruth Calder once read out the agreement of the five towns, believing it flooded or fallen, and wishing it set down once more before it goes under.

events.title: Cnoc thais taken
events.body: Cnoc thais is taken after the regiments cut the road to its pits. Tom Varley's two shafts are fired and sealed. The open record gives the number of holdouts taken, and not the number who went on into the hills.

events.title: Onto the windy coast
events.body: Some of the holdouts of Cnoc thais go on beyond the hills and out onto the windy coast of the far north-west. The regiments follow them to the edge of the shire of Seann Vell and no farther. The open record names them, as it names every foe of the war, only as those 'of no shire'.

events.body: The second fleet is raised at Seann Skell on the southern coast, to keep the eastern and southern waters while the first and fourth are in the north-west.

events.title: Raiders take the salt-boats
events.body: With the fleets drawn to the north-west, raiders from the eastern waters take two salt-boats off Àth bheag and burn a third. The second fleet runs down one of the raiders off Baile ìseal.

events.title: An siathamh rèisimeid raised
events.body: The sixth regiment is raised at Cnoc bheag, the great river port of the Hawk houses in the north-central country. It holds the northern road between the Tuathaich shires and the middle of the island, and the Hawk houses bless its colours by their own rite.

events.title: An dàrna rèisimeid raised
events.body: The second regiment is raised at Àth dhìreach in the east and set to guard the coal line and the library road. Its camp is the first soldiery the town of Muileann chaol has seen.

events.title: An ceathramh rèisimeid raised
events.body: The fourth regiment is raised at Caol bheag in the north-east. It goes down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar, is shipped west round the north coast in hired dubhan hulls, and is landed at Ceann mhòr in the Tuathaich north.

events.title: The regiments at Ceann mhòr
events.body: The fourth regiment is quartered at Ceann mhòr, in the old human magistrate's house that the maor has kept since the shires were drawn. The Moot protests the quartering. The protest is received.

events.title: The fishermen of Cathair gheal
events.body: The fleets off the north-west search the fishing boats of Cathair gheal on every day they put out. The fishermen petition the Moot, and the Moot petitions the council. The searching goes on.

events.title: An t-ochdamh rèisimeid raised
events.body: The eighth regiment is raised at Inis uaine on the Abhainn chaol in the east, to guard the dubhan depots and tanks of the eastern ports, which the council fears the holdouts may fire.

events.title: An treas cabhlach raised
events.body: The third fleet is raised at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast, and carries the army's dubhan up the west coast in tank-hulls to the regiments in the hills.

events.body: The Grey Night sect at Baile chrom keeps its vigil as always. The regiments quartered along the coast report a night when the whole town was dark and silent; they search it, and find nothing.

events.title: Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg
events.body: The last two western towns, Àth naomh and Tobar dhearg, open their roads to the regiments without a siege. Their pits are flooded. The open record names no holdouts taken at either.

events.body: In the last week of an Cèitean, with the road below Cnoc thais already cut, Tom Varley and Angus Rennie's cousin work out by lamplight how much powder will bring the lower galleries down clean and how much less would only crack the timbering.

events.body: The regiment below Cnoc thais spends the better part of a month digging and drilling before it finds a shepherd's path along the northern ridge too steep for anything but goats, which the town's own watchers had judged not worth the watching.

events.body: A trader named Cairstine, who has walked the coast path with salt and needles twice a year since before the war had a name, carries the season's word up to the fisherfolk and the seven parties both.

events.title: A fisherman's word on the door left open
events.body: A fisherman of Baile ìseal tells Cairstine that a kingdom which shuts a door on nothing much will find another door, one it did not think to watch, standing open behind it, and she carries the saying north with the rest of the season's news.

events.body: Through the autumn Tom Varley keeps, unwritten, a tally in his own head of the men who came out of Cnoc thais with him, the men the regiment marched south, and a field left unploughed below Àth leathan he cannot yet set down as finished.

events.body: In the last clear evening before the hard weather turns, Tom Varley stands on a strand of black shingle at the edge of an Oirthir Ghaothach and watches the light go out of the sky without any sunset to mark the day's end.

events.body: At the council of Cnoc thais in the chapel room an old widow, Mary Kessock, says a town threatened by soldiers it cannot fight may be taken whole or leave the takers nothing and go. The room begins to make ready to leave.

events.body: A widower of an Oirthir Ghaothach, Calum Odhar, who fishes a two-man boat out of a cove with no name, gives the byre behind his house to the six men of Cnoc thais and asks only whether they can mend a net.

events.title: Cnoc bhàn's harbour shut to strangers
events.body: The Tuathaich of Cnoc bhàn shut their harbour to boats they do not know through the autumn, fearing raiders with the fleets drawn to the north-west, and turn away a Dia-thìreach trader with a load of salt.

events.title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh watches the camp from her garden wall
events.body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, retired at Àth dhìreach, watches An dàrna rèisimeid's camp rise from her own garden wall and is asked by its young captain whether the wall marks ground his picket line needs; it does not. She notes the town gives the company no trouble and is given none.

events.title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh writes to Sìleas nic Rath of the camp
events.body: Beathag writes to Sìleas nic Rath that she trusts her own eyes on a garden wall better than she ever let herself trust the reports that once reached her desk from towns she had never stood in. The line is struck through once and left to stand, the ink thin enough to read beneath it.

events.title: The fourth marches down to the river
events.body: An ceathramh rèisimeid marches from Caol bheag to the river on a frosted morning, the whole town turned out along the road. Corporal Dùghall mac Iain's own mother stands at the mill corner and says nothing at all as he passes, which he takes, without either of them saying it, for the greater kindness.

events.title: The fourth's voyage down the Abhainn ghorm
events.body: An ceathramh rèisimeid goes down the Abhainn ghorm to Ros chiar in refitted coal barges, the two days' journey the maps had promised done in a day and a half on the autumn spate, the barge-men steering more than rowing, the men passing the crossing in games, arguments and a harvest song none of them had thought to sing.

events.title: The hired hulls put out from Ros chiar
events.body: An ceathramh rèisimeid's hired dubhan hulls put out from Ros chiar into a turning sea, five days round the north cape with the tanks below decks giving off a smell that does not leave the men's kit for weeks. A boy of the second company goes overboard reaching for a loosed line and is hauled back half-drowned.

events.title: One hull parts company off the north cape
events.body: In the worst of the second night's weather one of An ceathramh rèisimeid's hired hulls is separated from the rest, puts into a cove on the far side of the north cape, and loses two days finding the others again, reaching Ceann mhòr three days behind the rest with crew and cargo whole.

events.title: The maor of Ceann mhòr gives up his house
events.body: The maor of Ceann mhòr gives up the greater part of the old human magistrate's house to An ceathramh rèisimeid without complaint, moving his own household into its two upper rooms, and takes afterwards to walking their narrow gallery of an evening remarking to whichever officer passes below that the army has undone in a fortnight what forty winters of sea air had not.

events.title: The maor's clerk keeps the two tongues apart
events.body: The maor of Ceann mhòr's clerk, a Tuathaich woman of long service, addresses An ceathramh rèisimeid's captain in Dia-thìris without a stumble and her own townsfolk, on the office's business, in the humans' tongue alone, the two tongues kept, in her own ordering of things, for two entirely different kinds of transaction.

events.title: Martha Greaves's letter reaches the magistrate's house
events.body: Martha Greaves's single sheet asking that An ceathramh rèisimeid be lodged at its own charge and not the town's is carried up the coast road and read aloud by the fourth's own captain to his assembled company. It is received and forwarded; Comhairle nam Mèinnean's late reply says only that the arrangement stands until the campaign's needs change it.

events.title: The tongue Barbara Keir will not give him
events.body: Barbara answers Corporal Dùghall mac Iain readily in Dia-thìris on the house's own business, but gives him, try as he may, not one word of the humans' tongue, though he hears her speak it easily across the yard wall to a neighbour; he comes to understand it a door shut on him alone.

events.body: A week after its raising at Baile ghorm An treas cabhlach's first tank-hull, her number chalked on her bow for want of a name, comes into Ceann mhòr with the army's dubhan. events.title: A file sent north to Baile chrom
events.body: An ceathramh rèisimeid sends Corporal Dùghall mac Iain and six men on the two days' coast road to Baile chrom, a bent headland town no patrol of the regiment has yet troubled to search, with orders to look for arms and for men of the western hills and to bring back a report.

events.title: The watched mill on the coast road
events.body: On the march north the file passes a mill and two farms whose people watch them from their doorways and say nothing, a silence the soldier Cailean judges more telling, in its own way, than any shout a Dia-thìreach farm on the same road would have raised.

events.title: The town found dark and silent
events.body: Dùghall mac Iain's file comes into Baile chrom after dark on the eve of Oidhche Glaise to find no lamp lit, no dog loosed and every door unlatched; house after house holds a family sitting hands folded round a cold hearth, answering nothing but a single slow headshake.

events.title: Margaret Crane keeps the vigil alone
events.body: In the house nearest the lighthouse road an old woman named Margaret Crane sits alone keeping Oidhche Glaise as she has kept it since before the war, gives Dùghall mac Iain her name and leave to search, and tells him nothing more; a soldier of his own file sets his lamp down outside her door rather than carry its light past her.

events.title: The regimental clerk's question
events.body: Copying Dùghall mac Iain's report fair at the bothy, the file's young clerk asks whether there is more to the night than its three written lines; Dùghall tells him there is not, and keeps the headshakes and the cold hearths out of the regiment's own returns.

events.title: Barbara on the flooded pits
events.body: Dùghall mac Iain mentions the flooding of Àth naomh's pits to Barbara over her evening table; she answers only, in Dia-thìris, that a pit flooded is a pit flooded whichever order floods it, and takes up her mending again in the silence he has learned by then not to press.

events.title: Dùghall's sleepless winter
events.body: Through the short days that follow, Dùghall mac Iain wakes most nights with the sea-sound of the Baile chrom headland in his ears, unable in either tongue he carries to find words for a stillness that asked nothing of him and gave him nothing to answer with.

events.title: The column goes south
events.body: A column of holdouts, some hundreds strong, leaves the western hills and marches south-east through the middle of the island toward the capital. Why it did so is in the sealed archive. The Tuathaich tellings name its leader Owen Barrow. The open record gives no name.

events.title: The column's road
events.body: The column's road south-east runs by Àth bheag in the west, Muileann mhin and the edge of the capital's country. The towns it passes report it, and the open record copies their reports and not the regiments'.

events.title: The camp by Muileann ghlas
events.body: The column passes Muileann òg and camps on the fields by Muileann ghlas, a day's walk from Cathair dhearg. The first and third regiments are brought down the fair road to meet it.

events.body: The fair-ground at Muileann òg is cleared of its standing booths to give the first and third regiments room to camp. The books of its court for that year end with no closing entry.

events.title: Battle of Muileann ghlas
events.body: The second great battle of the war, and the last. In two summers of fighting the Tuathaich holdouts are broken: children of the humans once driven to the island's edge, driven back again, and this time by a fuel that one of their own devised.

events.title: The field at Muileann ghlas
events.body: The open record lists the first and third regiments on the field at Muileann ghlas and gives no count of the column's dead. The regiments' own dead are named on a stone at Cathair mhòr, set up the next year.

events.title: The last pits give up
events.body: Word of Muileann ghlas reaches the hills, and the holdouts still there come down to the posts of the seventh regiment on the Àth leathan road. They are disarmed and sent home. The open record counts their weapons.

events.title: An Cogadh Fada ends
events.body: The Long War ends. Nine regiments and four fleets were raised in it, each named for the town where it is stationed, and all of them stand to this day.

events.title: Fadachadh
events.body: Among Tuathaich speakers 'chaidh am fadachadh', they got long-warred, begins to be said of the defeat in the west, and then of any defeat after holding out too long. It is said as a jest, and those who say it do not laugh.

events.title: The pass at the Caol mhòr steps
events.body: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's office begins issuing a small paper against a name, a face and a stated errand for anyone at Caol mhòr who means to leave the harbour road; the town takes to calling it simply the pass, and Martha Greaves comes to show her own to the same soldier three times that spring on Moot business.

told_in.section: I. Of the Pass at the Harbour Wall

events.title: Joe Ashby's boats searched again
events.body: A patrol captain boards every hull at Caol mhòr's harbour wall in the last week of an Cèitean, the engine-boats last and most carefully; Joe Ashby, watching from his shed door, tells him plainly that no guild in the harbour would give him leave to fit them, and the captain writes it down without comment.

events.title: Joe Ashby fits a fleet hull again
events.body: Before the summer is out the depot's own men send for Joe Ashby a second time, for a hull no guild-trained fitter at Seann Skell could put right; he mends it, takes his coin at the harbour's own rate, and asks no more of the matter than the coin requires.

events.title: Tional nan Tuathach's register adds the names of Àth leathan
events.body: Peter Hale brings Martha Greaves a list gathered from the western towns under the disarming; she enters the dead and maimed of Àth leathan into Tional nan Tuathach's register column by column, and finds Ruth Calder's own name on none of its three columns.

events.title: Easter kept under watch
events.body: Martha Greaves stands at the back of Eaglais nan Tuathach's own Easter service at the chapel above Doire ghlas and finds a single soldier of the regiments posted at the door the whole length of it, writing nothing in his book, the service passing between door and altar without a word exchanged.

events.title: Ellen Marsh takes down the Cnoc thais women
events.body: In the schoolroom given over the autumn before, Ellen Marsh takes down the accounts of the women of Cnoc thais bench by bench for her twelfth book, among them Peggy Innes's telling of a farm that bakes a second loaf every night and leaves it on the sill for a coming and going the disarming never ended.

told_in.section: III. Of the Women from Cnoc thais

events.title: A hill farm burned above Cnoc thais
events.body: A patrol of the regiments finds a farm above Cnoc thais with a barn half full of grain no ration book can account for and burns the house and byre, turning the family into their own yard first; no one is killed, and Ellen Marsh sets the telling down in the same flat voice the women themselves use for it.

told_in.section: III. Of the Women from Cnoc thais

events.title: Ellen Marsh finishes her twelfth book
events.body: In the first week of an Dàmhair Ellen Marsh closes the twelfth of her books of Tuathaich accounts, the one that gathers the war her first eleven never spoke of, and writes on its last leaf that she does not know which of her twelve a reader two generations off will find the harder to believe.

events.title: An ceathramh rèisimeid's year of patrols on the Ceann mhòr road
events.body: Through the whole quartered year An ceathramh rèisimeid keeps its patrols on the Ceann mhòr road, a file out at first light and in at dusk; no arms and no unaccounted man are found, and the regiment's returns settle into the same three words that closed every report of the autumn before.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Hymn Through the Wall

events.title: Dùghall hears the hymn through the wall
events.body: Of an evening in an t-Sultain, Dùghall mac Iain hears through the wall of Barbara's house a hymn sung low in the humans' tongue, heavier than her shuttle-song of the autumn before; by an Dàmhair he can carry its whole shape in his head without meaning to have learned it, and catches himself humming it on the road.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Hymn Through the Wall

events.title: Cailean's own grandmother's tune
events.body: Dùghall mac Iain hums two bars of the learned hymn to the soldier Cailean over a cold supper; Cailean says his own grandmother kept a tune very like it, that he never asked its words either, and that a man billeted long enough on a house not his own generally carries some piece of it home in him.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Hymn Through the Wall

events.title: A rumour that will not run to ground
events.body: Across the quartered year a single rumour passes from the Cnoc thais hill paths to the Doire ghlas schoolroom to the Ceann mhòr road, that something gathers in the western hills the disarming never reached; no regiment's patrol and no clerk's report ever explains it, and it never twice is told the same way.

events.title: Word reaches Caol mhòr that the hills are moving
events.body: In the last week of an Dàmhair a Board carrier rides two days without pausing to bring Caol mhòr word that some hundreds have come down out of the western hills and turned south-east across the middle of the island; Martha Greaves reads the note beside her register's own closed column on the names of Àth leathan.

events.body: A carter of Caol mhòr shows his pass at the harbour steps in his mourning black to walk to his father's burial two roads inland, the office having made no separate provision for burials.

events.body: On the Ceann mhòr road a boy of ten driving three cows begins, in the second season of the patrols, to lift a hand to An ceathramh rèisimeid's file as it passes.

events.title: Bread left on a sill above Cnoc thais
events.body: A farm two ridges back from ruined Cnoc thais bakes twice what its household can eat and leaves the second baking on the sill overnight; the loaves are gone by morning and the sill is never watched.

events.body: Marion Kenny tells Ellen Marsh that the family of the burned farm above Cnoc thais were given time by the patrol to carry out a chest, a loom and the year's meal before the thatch was fired.

events.body: A clerk of Comhairle nam Mèinnean stationed at Cnoc thais writes to Tional nan Tuathach that the hill paths above the town carry more foot-traffic by night than any patrol's daylight count can explain.

events.body: The northern office sets a clerk with his grey passes in the old wool-hall at Cnoc ghorm; the Tuathaich come to him one household at a time, and the elders have their own names written first.

events.body: The regiments' lorries on the north road take on fuel at a pump set up in the yard of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta above Muileann fhada, the landlord renting the yard to Comhairle nam Mèinnean and keeping his wicks inside.

events.title: Àth bheag's report of the ford
events.body: The maor of Àth bheag writes the fullest report of the column's road: some four hundred men forded the water below the bridge at dawn, in order, without banner or drum, and went on south without stopping.

events.title: Muileann mhin's miller reports no loss
events.body: The miller of Muileann mhin under the western hills writes to Comhairle nam Mèinnean that the town's takings showed no loss by the column's passing, the bread having been paid for at a fair price and nobody's stock troubled beyond it.

events.body: A party of the column sleeps a night in Aonghas mac Cuinn's barn and leaves coin and a note under a stone, thanking him and asking nothing more.

events.title: The column keeps wide of the towns of the fair country
events.body: Crossing the open country toward the capital's fields, the column holds a road that passes no town of any size, and the small farms it crosses report only a quiet passing.

events.body: The miller's wife of Àth bheag, watching the column cross from the mill loft, says she saw no banner among them and no drum, only a man at the head whom the rest left the whole width of the road.

events.title: The column sings through its last night in the open
events.body: On the bank and in the thorn below Muileann ghlas the column keeps its last night before the battle by singing low, company after company, in part for what courage it lends and in part because there are children on the field with nowhere else on the island to be left.

told_in.section: II. Of the Tellings

events.title: Owen Barrow walks the line before first light
events.body: In the last hour of dark Owen Barrow goes the length of the column's line, speaking to each company and to many of the column by name; he is remembered in the north to have said that the hills lie behind them now and cannot be walked back to before the guns find them either way. An Clàr Foscailte names him nowhere.

events.title: The guns find the thorn stand
events.body: An treas rèisimeid's four field pieces, hauled the last two miles by hand through ground too soft for the horses, find the column's thorn-stand line within the first half-hour of the fighting; what holds after that holds along the bank itself, hand to hand, through most of the short forenoon.

events.title: A requisition for lime
events.body: The regiments' burial parties ask the quartermaster for a good deal more lime than three-and-twenty graves would need. The requisition survives where no count of the column's own dead does, and is the nearest thing An Clàr Foscailte holds to one.

told_in.section: I. Of the Field

events.title: The miller's wife keeps her kitchen through the battle
events.body: As the mill at Muileann ghlas changes hands twice before noon, the miller's wife will not leave her own kitchen for either army, and is remembered by the regiments' surgeon to have gone on moving her pots and sacks from whichever corner the fighting had just left.

told_in.section: I. Of the Field

events.title: The colonel's report
events.body: A' chiad rèisimeid's colonel writes that the column held the bank at Muileann ghlas longer than any force he had faced in two years of war, and sets it down, he says, only so his council should have the field's truth and not a prettier account of it.

told_in.section: I. Of the Field

events.title: The taken ground remembered
events.body: An old man of Muileann ghlas, brought before the regiments' officers to answer for a store of grain, tells them the field carries an older name, the taken ground, from a battle of Cogadh nam Bràithrean fought on the same ground two centuries before.

told_in.section: I. Of the Field

events.title: The sixty come out of the byres
events.body: After dark, some sixty of the column still holding the mill and its byres come out under a promise, carried by a Tuathach prisoner on a white cloth, that any man unarmed will be marched and not shot; they are counted, searched and held overnight on the mill floor.

told_in.section: I. Of the Field

events.title: The regiments' surgeon treats both sides alike
events.body: The regiments' own surgeon, two years out of his training, tends the wounded of both the regiments and the column through the night at Muileann ghlas by two lanterns and a banked fire, and An Clàr Foscailte notes that he made no distinction between them.

told_in.section: I. Of the Field

events.title: The old man of Cnoc thais brings down his cow
events.body: A lame old man of Cnoc thais comes down to An seachdamh rèisimeid's northernmost post on the Àth leathan road carrying no weapon, leading on a rope halter the one cow his family kept through two summers of war, and is let through with it.

events.title: The sergeant judges the counting done
events.body: At An seachdamh rèisimeid's northernmost post the sergeant keeping the list of the hills' people notes, when no one more has come down the road by noon, that he takes the empty road to mean the counting is finished.

told_in.section: III. Of the Roads Home

events.title: Somhairle hears the guns are done
events.body: Somhairle mac Lachlainn hears at the capital, from a clerk who comes into his room without knocking, that the fighting at Muileann ghlas is over; he says afterward that his first thought was for Slighe a' Ghuail's timetable and the wounded's carriage north.

told_in.section: IV. Of Somhairle After

events.title: Somhairle checks the wounded trains twice over
events.body: In the first weeks of the peace Somhairle mac Lachlainn has Slighe a' Ghuail's schedule for the war's wounded checked twice against the surgeons' own returns, to be sure no man carried north that winter rode on a train meant for other cargo.

told_in.section: IV. Of Somhairle After

events.title: Near ninety of the column's wounded brought in
events.body: The regiments' surgeon's tally for the night after Muileann ghlas stands at twenty-three of the regiments buried or dying and near ninety of the column's wounded brought in.

told_in.section: I. Of the Field

events.title: Taigh-solais Àth dhearg sees no fleet
events.body: The keeper of Taigh-solais Àth dhearg on the north-east cape writes in his log through the autumn that no ship of the fleets has passed the cape in three months.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Near ninety of the column's wounded brought in

told_in.section: I. Of the Field

events.title: The regiments stay on their stations
events.body: The nine regiments and four fleets are not stood down. The council keeps each at the town where it was raised and pays them from the wartime tithe.

events.title: The market charter of Caol ruadh
events.body: Caol ruadh, whose harbour victualled the garrisons and the second fleet through the war, is granted a market right for the southern strait. It is the sixteenth market town, and the last chartered.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first market under the Caol ruadh charter

events.title: Dubhan's fuel over all the island
events.body: With the last ordered resistance gone, Dubhan's fuel is in all but law compelled upon the whole trade of the island.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Comhairle nam Mèinnean ends the coal trade outside An Sloc Mòr

events.title: The western seams flooded
events.body: By the Board's order the last western seams are flooded and their shafts capped with concrete. The seventh regiment stands by at every capping. After this no coal is dug on the island outside the Board's own works.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first capping at Àth leathan

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Sergeant Iain Mòr counts the cappings

events.title: The prisoners sent home
events.body: The holdouts held since Muileann ghlas are let out of the capital's gaol and sent north under guard of the first regiment as far as the boundary stones. The Moot's register adds their names, in a column of their own, to the dead and maimed it has kept since the Severance.

events.title: Somhairle mac Lachlainn seated
events.body: Somhairle mac Lachlainn is given a seat on the council, the first soldier to sit there since the captains of the Severance war.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Anna nic Phàil speaks to Somhairle at the chamber door

events.title: The seventh regiment at Àth leathan
events.body: The seventh regiment builds a post on the road below Àth leathan and keeps a company there. In the regimental lists it is called the Àth leathan post, and in the town something else.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An seachdamh rèisimeid's first winter at the post

events.title: The stone at Cathair mhòr
events.body: A stone is set up at Cathair mhòr bearing the names of the regiments' dead from Àth leathan and Muileann ghlas. It stands beside the market cross of the house of Mac Ùisdein.

events.title: The Muileann ghlas field
events.body: The field at Muileann ghlas where the column camped is sown again. For years the farmer who holds it finds weapons in the furrows and hands them to the first regiment, which keeps a list.

events.title: The first capping at Àth leathan
events.body: In am Màrt An seachdamh rèisimeid pours the first concrete over a flooded shaft at Àth leathan while Somhairle mac Lachlainn watches from the pit-head; the mix lies still in a way the seam itself, even flooded, had never once lain before.

told_in.section: I. Of the Capping

events.title: Sergeant Iain Mòr counts the cappings
events.body: A sergeant of An seachdamh rèisimeid tells Somhairle mac Lachlainn this is the fourth capping his company has stood by that month, at Muileann àrsaidh, Cnoc thais and a nameless working near Àth naomh, and wonders aloud what the regiment will be set to guard once Tobar dhearg of the hills is done.

events.title: Comhairle nam Mèinnean ends the coal trade outside An Sloc Mòr
events.body: Fearghas mac Aonghais's office notes that the trade in coal-fuel is at an end on the island outside what Comhairle nam Mèinnean still cuts for its own account at An Sloc Mòr: not forbidden by any law, but ended by there being, at last, nowhere left to sell it.

events.title: Aonghas mac Phàdraig's plough finds the first iron
events.body: Turning his field at Muileann ghlas in am Màrt as he has every spring of his life, Aonghas mac Phàdraig's share brings up a rusted bayonet lying whole across it; he finishes the furrow before he carries it home.

events.title: A' chiad rèisimeid's corporal begins a list
events.body: A corporal of A' chiad rèisimeid collecting rents in the district takes Aonghas mac Phàdraig's bayonet and enters it on a list kept for such finds, not knowing whether it is a record of the dead or only of the field giving back what two armies left in it.

events.title: The letter from the capital's gaol
events.body: Martha Greaves receives word from the council's office that the holdouts taken at Muileann ghlas are to be released in an t-Iuchar and marched north to the boundary stones, with no word of who is to feed them on the road or what their flooded towns will make of their return.

events.title: A man refuses his name for a town that no longer stands
events.body: An older prisoner at the boundary stones will not give his name at first, saying it would mean nothing written beside Muileann àrsaidh's ruin; Martha Greaves promises the town will stand again in whatever shape its people build it, and he gives his name.

events.title: Peter Hale keeps a name of his own
events.body: Among the released Peter Hale recognises a man once apprenticed to the same binder at Muileann leathan whose pupils rebound Tional nan Tuathach's minute-books; the man gives no sign of knowing him, and Peter does not ask which it is, silence or forgetting.

events.title: Anna nic Phàil speaks to Somhairle at the chamber door
events.body: At the close of his first sitting Anna nic Phàil tells Somhairle mac Lachlainn she stood on the bench in the passage an Nollaig Martha Greaves carried Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail in, and means to go on voting every mercy the council's business allows her.

told_in.section: III. Of the Seat and the Post

events.title: Somhairle reads the one-and-sixty names
events.body: At the stone's unveiling at Cathair mhòr, Somhairle mac Lachlainn reads aloud the one-and-sixty names of the regiments' dead from Àth leathan and Muileann ghlas to a silent square, and finds the town's silence harder to bear than any noise it might have made instead.

told_in.section: IV. Of the Stone and the Sown Field

events.title: Somhairle thinks of the names the stone does not carry
events.body: Standing alone at the stone after the crowd disperses, Somhairle mac Lachlainn counts over the column's uncounted dead, the sixty from the byres, and a mother's son who was not among the released, and finds that number, cut nowhere, stays with him longer than the one that is.

events.title: Four score released at the boundary stones
events.body: Some four score holdouts taken at Muileann ghlas are handed to Tional nan Tuathach at the boundary stones; Martha Greaves writes their names in a column Peter Hale ruled that morning.

events.title: Two brothers of Seann Bhral on the stone
events.body: Among the names read at the stone's unveiling are two brothers of Seann Bhral who enlisted together and died within the same hour of the same morning.

events.body: An seachdamh rèisimeid's first winter at the post by Àth leathan is spent roofing it; the men buy their slates at the western Seann Skell.

events.title: The first market under the Caol ruadh charter
events.body: The first market held under Caol ruadh's new charter is held in the rain on the quay; the market-due is taken by a clerk of An t-Ionmhas under a sailcloth awning, and the fishwives sell out before noon.

events.title: A plough-share of Muileann ghlas
events.body: The farmer of the sown field at Muileann ghlas brings the first blade turned up by his plough to the regiments' post, and the corporal enters it in a book kept for the purpose.

events.title: The library's war archive sealed
events.body: The whole record of the Long War at Leabharlann Muileann chaol is sealed against all readers for fifty years. No other archive in the kingdom's history has been sealed.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The council's order reaches Muileann chaol

events.title: Sìleas nic Rath's open chronicle
events.body: Of the royal chronicle for the war years there stays open only Sìleas nic Rath's list of places, the regiments present and the counts she was allowed. Her full record went into the sealed archive with the rest.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Sìleas carries her full record to the door

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Sìleas's promise at the head of the open list

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Sìleas opens the next day's page as any other

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Some forty places on the open list

events.title: The cairn at Àth leathan
events.body: Tuathaich families build a cairn on the field of Àth leathan without leave. The patrols of the seventh regiment leave it standing, and every time they pass it has grown by a stone or two.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: An seachdamh rèisimeid's captain lets the cairn stand

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A woman of Àth leathan carries a stone each morning

events.title: The tithe carried forward
events.body: The Treasury's accounts carry the wartime tithe forward as a standing line under the regiments' pay. No minute of the council records a choice to keep it.

events.title: The market-due fixed
events.body: The Treasury fixes the market-due at seventeen in the hundred on every sale a town makes into its market and on every sale between markets. A clerk of the Treasury is set in each of the sixteen market towns to take it and keep the market roll. The wartime tithe on dubhan stays at the pumps, on its own line.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Doire shean pays the market-due

events.title: The Fuel-Fitters and the regiments
events.body: The Guild of Fuel-Fitters at Seann Skell on the southern coast is given the contract for the regiments' engines and the fleets' hulls, and doubles its rolls. The charter rule holds, and all its new fitters are Dia-thìrich.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Peigi nic Ascaill signs the regiments' contract

events.title: The regiments' arms contracts
events.body: The forges of Àth naomh in the west and Caol ìseal on the north coast, which smelt the bog-iron of their districts, take the Crown's contract for the regiments' small arms and field-guns. The forge-towns of the old vein country follow. Arms become the dearest common goods in every market of the kingdom.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A smith of Àth naomh counts his musket-stocks

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The forge at Caol ìseal takes on new hands

events.title: The second fleet off Baile ìseal
events.body: The second fleet runs down off Baile ìseal the raiders who took the salt-boats in the war, and brings their hulls into Seann Skell. The lighthouse log at Baile ìseal records the chase from the lamp-room.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seonag nic Thòmais lights the second lamp

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Cnoc bhàn's harbour opened again

events.title: The fourth fleet in the north-west
events.body: The fourth fleet, kept on the Tuathaich coast after the war, searches the raiders' bays off Cathair gheal and finds them empty. The fishermen of Cathair gheal say the raiders left when the fleets came and will return when they go.

events.title: The third fleet's tank-hulls
events.body: The third fleet at Baile ghorm keeps its tank-hulls after the war and runs dubhan up the west coast to the Tuathaich depots on the council's contract. The Moot pays the freight.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The quays of Baile ghorm lengthened

events.title: The council's order reaches Muileann chaol
events.body: A rider who has changed horses three times brings the council's four-line order to Raghnall mac Mhuirich on the doorstep of the old building: the whole record of An Cogadh Fada is to be shut against every reader for fifty years, and the keeper alone is to hold the key.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The library's war archive sealed

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Raghnall has a room built for the seal

told_in.section: I. Of the Key

events.title: Raghnall has a room built for the seal
events.body: Raghnall clears an old storeroom at the end of the new wing's gallery and has a mason and a smith fit it, through a fortnight of hard weather, with an oak door two inches thick and a lock made new to no other key in the kingdom, standing over the last morning's fitting himself.

links.title: The library's war archive sealed

links.title: The council's order reaches Muileann chaol

told_in.section: I. Of the Key

events.title: Sìleas carries her full record to the door
events.body: Over two days Sìleas nic Rath carries her own four boxes of the war's full record up from her room and sets them inside the new door herself, letting no clerk touch them: the movements, counts and letters she was never let publish alongside the open chronicle.

told_in.section: I. Of the Key

events.title: The key turns once
events.body: Raghnall turns the new lock himself with the mason and smith gone, and hangs the key on a cord under his own shirt, where he is seen for years after to lay his hand against his chest before he blows out the reading-room's last lamp.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The library's war archive sealed

told_in.section: I. Of the Key

events.title: Sìleas's promise at the head of the open list
events.body: Sìleas writes, unasked, a line at the head of the war's open list saying plainly that the fuller record exists, is kept, and will be given to any honest reader when the fifty years end; Raghnall reads it and lets it stand.

events.title: An seachdamh rèisimeid's captain lets the cairn stand
events.body: Asked whether to clear the cairn the Tuathaich have raised on Àraich Àth leathan, Comhairle nam Mèinnean answers that its captain may use his own judgment; he tells his patrols to walk past it and count the stones if they wish, and report only what is found beneath one.

events.title: A woman of Àth leathan carries a stone each morning
events.body: A woman of the town who lost a brother in the fighting there, and will not say which side he died fighting for, is seen to walk out alone before the patrol each morning, set one stone on the cairn, and stand a while with her hand flat against it before going home.

events.title: Peigi nic Ascaill signs the regiments' contract
events.body: Peigi nic Ascaill signs Comann nan Goibhnean-ceangail' contract for the regiments' engines and the fleets' hulls at Cathair dhearg with a clerk on either hand to witness it, and tells her under-fitter afterward that no paper she has signed will put more Dia-thìrich fitters to the trade than this one.

events.title: A smith of Àth naomh counts his musket-stocks
events.body: Writing to his brother at Cathair dhearg, a smith of Àth naomh says he has turned out more musket-stocks that winter than ploughshares in the six years before the war, and cannot decide whether to call it his own good fortune or the kingdom's bad one.

events.title: The forge at Caol ìseal takes on new hands
events.body: The woman who masters the forge at Caol ìseal, left her by a father with no son to leave it to, takes on four boys and a girl under the arms contract and tells Comhairle nam Mèinnean's inspector she means to keep them past the contract's term, war or no war.

events.title: Seonag nic Thòmais lights the second lamp
events.body: Keeper of the trial lamp at Baile ìseal, Seonag nic Thòmais sees the salt-boat raiders' sail two hours before An dàrna cabhlach's own lookout and lights, on her own judgment, the warning lamp kept unlit in ordinary weather; the fleet's captain copies her log whole into his return.

events.title: Sìleas opens the next day's page as any other
events.body: The morning after the lock is turned, Sìleas sets the day's date and the weather at the top of her page and writes only of a mill's copying fee, exactly as on any working morning of the thirteen years before, and says nothing there of the sealed room.

events.title: Some forty places on the open list
events.body: The open list of the war years at an Leabharlann runs to some forty places, each with its regiments and the counts allowed before the sealing, and a blank where the column's dead would stand.

events.title: The quays of Baile ghorm lengthened
events.body: For An treas cabhlach's tank-hulls the quays of Baile ghorm are lengthened by forty paces into the anchorage, the stone carted from the old wolf-posts' quarry.

events.title: Doire shean pays the market-due
events.body: At Doire shean the fixed market-due is taken for the first time; Am Buabhall Fortanach, which sells no goods at market, is found to owe it on its buffalo.

events.title: Còmhrag Ceann leathan of Ceann leathan after the war
events.body: At the first Còmhrag at Ceann leathan after the last pits gave up, the fair-wardens count more fighters from the shires of the middle country than in any year before, and none from the western hills.

events.title: The creature off the cape again
events.body: The fourth fleet's log for the year records a thing longer than a patrol boat off the north-west cape, where the Tuathaich fishermen reported one in Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's day. The log calls it a whale.

events.title: Anna nic Phàil's motion
events.body: The motion to make amends to the Tuathaich is brought into the council by Anna nic Phàil, councillor for Cathair dhomhain, on a petition of the Moot under Martha Greaves. She speaks for it once.

events.title: The motion for amends
events.body: In the capital it is proposed to pay the Tuathaich for their losses in the war. The motion is let die quietly, and no vote is taken.

events.title: The Moot's minute on the amends
events.body: The Moot's minute on the motion for amends runs to one line: 'Allowed to die.' That same year Martha Greaves lays down the chair. The Moot chooses Peter Hale, a great-grandson of its first speaker, to follow her.

events.title: The fifth regiment's barracks
events.body: The fifth regiment builds stone barracks at Seann Warr, the first lasting quarters any of the nine regiments has had. The town gives the land and takes the regiment's custom.

links.title: The quarrymen of Seann Warr

events.title: The eighth regiment at Inis uaine
events.body: The eighth regiment's guard on the eastern dubhan tanks at Inis uaine is made lasting. Its officers take houses in the town, and the Seann Spioradan house of Inis uaine adds the regiment to its prayers.

links.title: Officers' houses at Inis uaine

events.title: The fourth regiment leaves Ceann mhòr
events.body: The fourth regiment leaves the old magistrate's house at Ceann mhòr and goes home to Caol bheag. The Moot asks that the house be given to the town. It is given to the maor.

events.title: Anna nic Phàil cuts a page of figures from her own draft
events.body: Writing her motion at her own table through the early months of the year, Anna nic Phàil cuts a whole page of named costs, granaries and flooded pit-heads and Clach nan Rèisimeidean, judging that a council grows deaf to a column of figures faster than to almost anything else brought before it.

events.body: Uisdean Dubh, master of An t-Ionmhas, asks Anna nic Phàil's Tagradh na h-Èirig whether its sum has been costed against the year's roll; she answers that the reckoning is the room's own trade, and asks only that the principle be granted.

events.title: Somhairle mac Lachlainn is asked whether the sum is too great
events.body: Caught at the chamber door, Somhairle mac Lachlainn tells Anna nic Phàil that he has read many rolls of the dead and never once been asked whether the towns that raised them could bear the cost, and does not know why a roll of the dead should be easier to pay for than a roll of the living.

events.body: On the eighth day Tagradh na h-Èirig is absent from the business-paper; a clerk tells Anna nic Phàil it was stood over to the autumn sitting the evening before, in a short session she was not told was sitting, by members' vote without her among them.

events.title: Anna counts the councillors who looked away
events.body: Going back over the eight sittings, Anna nic Phàil can find no single vote that killed the motion, only the faces of the twelve, one who promised a vote and never called it, one who spoke of hard times, six who said nothing to her at all, and Somhairle who gave her an answer and moved no more than the rest to call it to a vote.

events.title: Martha Greaves tells Peter Hale she means to lay the chair down
events.body: In the delegates' room over the net-lofts at Caol mhòr, Martha Greaves tells Peter Hale plainly that she means to lay down Tional nan Tuathach's chair that year, and that she judges him, of every delegate she has sat among, the fittest to take it up.

events.title: Martha Greaves's last sitting
events.body: Martha Greaves reads out the year's register and the ordinary business of the day, a roof at the school, the price of wool, a mill's complaint of the coal-line's freight, lays the chair down, and Tional nan Tuathach chooses Peter Hale by acclamation without a show of hands.

events.title: Martha Greaves goes home to Doire ghlas
events.body: Martha Greaves rides home to Doire ghlas on the ordinary carrier's cart with no more baggage than she came to the mill with as a young woman, not yet certain what a woman who was Tional nan Tuathach's own voice for seventeen years is to do with her mornings now.

events.body: By council order An t-ochdamh rèisimeid's officers at Inis uaine are given houses in the town in place of quarters borrowed year by year from the tank-yard's sheds.

events.body: The quarrymen of Seann Warr cut the stone for An còigeamh rèisimeid's barracks through the summer from the same face that gave the harbour wall, and are paid by An t-Ionmhas at a rate the town's masons call fair.

events.body: The Tuathaich of Cnoc bhàn open their harbour again to boats they do not know, the raiders who took the salt-boats having been brought into Seann Skell.

events.title: The springs of Muileann ruadh in a wet summer
events.body: Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh run so full in the wet summer that the bath-house's lower room floods, and the custodians carry the sick up to the long room.

events.title: Seann-chunntas
events.body: Tuathaich speakers begin to name the tabled request to the library and the dead motion for amends together as 'seann-chunntas', an old reckoning that none in power will settle and none has cancelled. The Dia-thìrich in office do not take up the word.

events.body: The Mine Board shuts the upper galleries of the Sloc Mòr at Achadh dhomhain. One face is kept open in the Rite's keeping, to cut coal for the altars, a few baskets a year.

events.title: The last hewers
events.body: Twelve hewers are kept at the Sloc Mòr to cut the altar-coal in the Rite's keeping. They are the last of their trade to work the vein on the island, and the Rite gives them its own oath, not the dissolved guild's.

events.title: The regiments at the Còmhrag
events.body: Fighters of the regiments are entered in the Còmhrag at Ceann leathan for the first time. The ninth regiment's man wins it. The fair-wardens raise the gate-price again.

links.label: Leads to

events.title: The second regiment's library guard
events.body: The second regiment at Àth dhìreach keeps a guard at Leabharlann Muileann chaol over the sealed war archive. The keeper, Raghnall mac Mhuirich, writes to the council that the library did not ask for one.

events.title: The coal line carries no coal
events.body: The last coal train runs from Achadh dhomhain to Cathair dhearg. The coal line keeps its name and carries dubhan, wool and soldiers.

events.body: The sixth regiment at Cnoc bheag keeps posts on the northern road where the boundary stones stand. For the first time since the Severance the Tuathaich going south must show a pass. The council's minute calls the passes for a time only.

events.title: The fair of the present year
events.body: The fair at Muileann òg draws traders from every shire the state holds. Tuathaich wool is sold there on its northern day, through Dia-thìrich factors, as it has been since the first fair.

events.title: The dubhan works of the present
events.body: Dubhan is made at Seann Skell on the southern coast and at works in the east and north. Every lamp, engine, ship and lorry on the island runs on it. The coin is pegged to it, and the tithe is taken on every sale.

events.title: The Treasury's roll of the present year
events.body: The Treasury's roll for the year stands at 9,568 purses: 6,375 from the head-due, taken at eighteen purses on every five thousand heads, and 3,193 from the market-due, taken at seventeen in the hundred on every sale. The wartime tithe is carried on its own line under the regiments' pay. The windy coast pays neither due.

events.title: Dubhan's charter of export
events.body: Dubhan, who made the first working fuel and is now in his sixty-ninth year, wins from the council at Cathair dhearg, after a year of letters and three sittings, leave to sell dubhan beyond the island. It is the first leave the kingdom has given since the Severance for any good of Dia-thìr to pass beyond its waters. The charter is narrow. The Treasury sets each year's measure. The fuel is loaded only at Ros dhomhain, where a clerk of the Treasury takes the tithe on every barrel. The kingdom's depots and the Moot's are served first. Nothing of the vein goes with it: the vein's coal is not sold, and the custodians of Òrd Bhrìde seal every hold. Dubhan has told neither the council nor the chronicler who buys from him. In the autumn the first tank-hull loaded under the charter goes out past the north-western capes, and on the day she sails the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell say their prayer to keep the sea shut.

events.title: The present
events.body: The coal is all but gone. The trade of the island runs on a name that once belonged to one man. The Dia-thìrich hold the capital and the sea. The Tuathaich hold the north, a grievance five years old, their Church, and the memory of the First Canoe, Naomh Breandan's voyage to the Isle of the Blessed, which the people who have twice defeated them still call folklore.

events.title: The telling of the fire in the canoe
events.body: On the shortest day Ellen Marsh tells the eldest children at Doire ghlas the telling of A' Chiad Churach and of the fire its crew carried in a clay pot through the mist.

events.body: Sìleas nic Rath leaves Eachdraidh na Rìoghachd open on its stand at the year's end with the ink dry, as Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh had done before her.

events.title: Cnoc ghorm's elders at the northern posts
events.body: Elders of Cnoc ghorm going south to the fair show their passes at An siathamh rèisimeid's posts by the boundary stones, and write in their own book that the sergeant wished them a good road.

events.title: An Taigh-òsta Grianach in the present year
events.body: An Taigh-òsta Grianach at Cnoc dhìreach sells fuel at its yard, beds under its roof and suppers by a dubhan lamp, and its sign still names all three.
